R.q:
The bus pulled up to the clinic at 8:02. A woman in a red coat stepped off first, holding a toddler on her hip. She walked to the front desk and set down a folder. "We have a nine o'clock with Dr. Lee," she said. The receptionist glanced at the clock, then at the folder. "You're early," she said. "Have a seat." The woman sat down by the window. The toddler pressed his hand against the glass and watched the bus pull away.

Which point of view does the author use?
o: third person limited
first person
third person omniscient
third person objective
R.w: The narrator reports only what could be seen and heard (arrivals, movements and dialogue) and never reveals any character's thoughts or feelings. That is third-person objective.

n.0: A limited narrator would reveal one character's thoughts, such as why the woman came early; none are given.
n.1: "We" and "you" appear only inside the dialogue. The narrator never speaks as "I."
n.2: An omniscient narrator would reveal several characters' thoughts; this narrator reveals none.

R.q:
In a 12-week study, 60 adults who walked briskly for 30 minutes a day lowered their average resting heart rate from 76 to 70 beats per minute. A comparison group of 60 adults who kept their usual routines showed no change. After the study ended, researchers checked on the walkers for another 12 weeks. Walkers who stopped their daily walks returned to about their starting heart rates by the end of that period, while those who kept walking stayed near 70.

Lena was one of the walkers, and she plans to stop walking when the study ends. Based on the passage, what will most likely happen to her resting heart rate over the next 12 weeks?
o: It will probably stay near 70 because she completed the full 12 weeks of walking.
It will keep falling below 70 because the benefits of walking build over time.
It will rise above 76 because stopping exercise suddenly strains the heart.
It will probably drift back toward the rate she had before the study.
R.w: The follow-up found that walkers who stopped returned to about their starting heart rates within 12 weeks. Lena fits that group, so her rate should drift back toward where it began.

n.0: Staying near 70 applied to walkers who kept walking, not to those who stopped.
n.1: The passage shows no further drop after walking stops; this reverses the follow-up finding.
n.2: Walkers who stopped returned to about their starting rates; nothing suggests they rose above them.

R.q:
Read the description of the floor plan.

First Floor, Wellness Center
The main entrance is in the south wall and opens into the lobby. The reception desk stands against the north wall of the lobby, facing the entrance. From the east side of the lobby, a hallway runs north. Along the hallway's east side are Exam Room 1, Exam Room 2 and Exam Room 3, in that order from south to north. On the hallway's west side, directly across from Exam Room 2, is the lab. The restrooms are at the far north end of the hallway. West of the lobby is the pharmacy, which has its own outside door in the west wall.

Based on the floor plan, which room is closest to the restrooms?
o: Exam Room 3
Exam Room 1
The pharmacy
The lab
R.w: The restrooms are at the north end of the hallway. Exam Room 3 is the farthest north of the rooms along the hallway, so it is closest.

n.1: Exam Room 1 is the farthest south along the hallway, nearest the lobby.
n.2: The pharmacy is west of the lobby, on the opposite side of the building from the hallway.
n.3: The lab sits across from Exam Room 2, in the middle of the hallway, south of Exam Room 3.

R.q:
Follow the directions.

A clinic scheduler uses these steps to set a follow-up time. Start with 8:50 a.m. and carry out the steps in order, applying each step to the result of the step before it.
1. Add 3 hours and 25 minutes.
2. If the time is now later than 12:00 noon, subtract 50 minutes; otherwise, add 50 minutes.
3. Move the time forward to the next quarter hour (:00, :15, :30 or :45), unless it is already on one.
4. Add 1 hour and 40 minutes.

What is the final time?
R.w: Step 1: 8:50 a.m. + 3:25 = 12:15 p.m. Step 2: 12:15 p.m. is later than noon, so subtract 50 minutes: 11:25 a.m. Step 3: forward to the next quarter hour: 11:30 a.m. Step 4: 11:30 a.m. + 1:40 = 1:10 p.m.

n.0: Takes the wrong branch in step 2 (adding 50 minutes to get 1:05 p.m.), then 1:15 p.m., then 2:55 p.m.
n.3: Rounds back to 11:15 a.m. in step 3 instead of forward to 11:30 a.m.

R.q:
The new scheduling plan was met with tepid support at the staff meeting. A few nurses nodded politely, but no one volunteered to help test it, and the sign-up sheet posted outside the break room stayed nearly empty for a week. The unit manager decided to delay the change until she could gather more feedback.

As used in the passage, the word tepid most nearly means
o: quiet but loyal.
openly hostile.
slightly warm.
unenthusiastic.
R.w: Polite nods, no volunteers and an empty sign-up sheet describe support that exists but lacks energy. Here tepid means unenthusiastic or halfhearted.

n.0: No one acts on the plan, so the context shows weak support, not loyalty.
n.1: No one objects or argues; polite nodding is the opposite of open hostility.
n.2: "Slightly warm" is the literal dictionary meaning, used for liquids; it does not fit support for a plan.

R.q:
Read the passage.

In April, the city of Fairview painted protected bike lanes on six blocks of Main Street, replacing a row of parking spaces. The pilot was scheduled to run for six months.

During the pilot, the number of cyclists counted on Main Street each weekday doubled, and the city recorded no bicycle crashes on those blocks, compared with four in the same months of the previous year. Several shop owners said that losing parking had cut into their sales, although city sales-tax records showed little change for the area.

The city council will vote in November on whether to make the lanes permanent.

Which summary of the passage is the most objective?
o: Fairview's bike lane pilot doubled cycling with no crashes; some shops reported lost sales, and a council vote is pending.
Fairview's bike lanes hurt Main Street shops by removing parking, in exchange for a modest rise in the number of cyclists.
Fairview's successful bike lane pilot doubled cycling and ended crashes on Main Street, so the council should keep the lanes.
Fairview's bike lane pilot was so popular with cyclists that the council has decided to make the Main Street lanes permanent.
R.w: An objective summary restates the main points without taking sides or adding information. This option reports the results, the shop owners' complaint and the pending vote, all as the passage presents them.

n.1: Slanted: it presents the shop owners' claim as fact, though tax records showed little change, and calls a doubling "modest."
n.2: Adds the writer's judgment ("successful," "should keep the lanes"), which makes the summary an opinion.
n.3: Inaccurate: the council has not decided anything; the passage says the vote will happen in November.

R.q:
The town of Kellerton opened a skate park near downtown last spring. In the twelve months that followed, police reports of vandalism downtown fell by 25 percent. The year before, downtown business owners had complained about broken windows and graffiti on at least a dozen buildings. The mayor says the skate park gave teenagers a place to go and caused the drop, and she wants to build a second park on the east side.

Which of the following, if true, would weaken the mayor's argument? Select all that apply.
o: The skate park cost less to build than the town had budgeted.
Vandalism reports fell by a similar amount in nearby towns without skate parks.
That spring, police began counting several incidents at one site as one report.
The town installed security cameras downtown in the same year.
Downtown business owners say the area has felt safer at night since the park opened.
Teenagers make up most of the skate park's daily visitors, especially after school.
R.w: Cameras offer another cause, a similar regional drop suggests a trend unrelated to the park, and a change in how reports are counted could lower the numbers without any real change in vandalism. Each gives a reason to doubt the park caused the drop.

n.0: Building cost has no bearing on whether the park reduced vandalism.
n.4: Owners feeling safer is loosely consistent with the mayor's claim and does not offer another cause.
n.5: Teens using the park fits the mayor's explanation and does not weaken it.

R.q:
Passage 1
A young beaver tried to build a dam alone. Each night the current carried away his branches, and each morning he began again, too proud to call the older beavers downstream. At last, worn out, he asked. By sunset, five of them had built what he had failed to build in a week.

Passage 2
In her first month as a new graduate nurse, Kim stayed late every night to finish her charting. She was sure that asking her preceptor for shortcuts would look weak. When she finally asked, her preceptor showed her how to chart at the bedside, and Kim began leaving on time. "I wish I had asked in week one," she said.

Which theme is developed in both passages?
o: Pride can keep people from help that would make their work easier.
Experienced workers should seek out newcomers who need training.
Working longer hours is the surest way to master a new task.
Animals and people learn new skills in very different ways.
R.w: The beaver is too proud to ask the older beavers, and Kim fears that asking will look weak. In both, asking finally solves the problem, so both develop the idea that pride blocks useful help.

n.1: Neither text says experienced workers should seek out newcomers; in both, the newcomer finally asks.
n.2: Both texts show long hours failing; success comes from asking for help.
n.3: The passages show the beaver and Kim learning the same lesson, so they are parallel, not contrasted.

R.q:
Read the job posting.

Help Wanted: Certified Nursing Assistant (CNA)
Willow Creek Senior Living is hiring full-time and part-time CNAs for day and evening shifts. Requirements: current state CNA certification, CPR certification (or willingness to obtain it within 30 days of hire), and the ability to lift 50 pounds. One year of experience is preferred but not required. Pay starts at $18.50 per hour, with an extra $2.00 per hour for evening shifts and $1.50 per hour for weekend shifts. Full-time staff receive health insurance after 60 days. Apply online or in person, Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Jada holds a current state CNA certification but does not yet have CPR certification or any work experience. She plans to work evening shifts on weekdays. Based on the posting, what would her starting hourly pay be?
R.w: Jada qualifies: CPR can be obtained within 30 days, and experience is preferred, not required. Her base pay is $18.50, plus $2.00 for evening shifts, for $20.50. She works weekdays, so the weekend bonus does not apply.

n.1: Adds the $1.50 weekend addition instead of the $2.00 evening addition.
n.2: Adds both the evening and the weekend additions, but Jada works weekdays.
n.3: Leaves out the $2.00 evening shift addition.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Marcus had rehearsed his speech for the scholarship committee a dozen times in front of the bathroom mirror. When he walked into the room, though, the five faces at the long table made his notes feel like someone else's words. He stumbled through the first paragraph, then stopped. For a long moment he said nothing. Then he folded the paper and told them about the winter his grandmother was sick, when he had learned to check her blood sugar and cook her meals before school, and how that winter had made him want to become a nurse. When he finished, one committee member was writing quickly, and another nodded. Outside, Marcus realized he could not remember a single line of the speech he had practiced.

Which is the best summary of the passage?
o: One winter Marcus cared for his sick grandmother before school, which made him want to become a nurse.
Nervous, Marcus abandoned his rehearsed speech and spoke from experience, which seemed to engage the panel.
Marcus won a nursing scholarship after he told the committee a moving story about his grandmother.
Marcus practiced a scholarship speech many times but forgot most of it when he faced the committee.
R.w: The passage moves from Marcus's preparation, to his loss of confidence, to his decision to speak from personal experience, to the committee's positive reaction. This option covers that whole arc without adding events.

n.0: This is the backstory Marcus tells, a detail inside the story rather than a summary of the passage.
n.2: Goes beyond the text: the committee seemed engaged, but the passage never says Marcus won the scholarship.
n.3: Covers only the first part of the story and leaves out what Marcus did instead and how the committee responded.

R.q:
Ever since the new neighbor moved in, Mrs. Abbott has watched him from behind her curtains. "He's a scrawny young man," she told her sister, "and nosy, too. He asked me how long I'd lived here." Her sister laughed. "He sounds curious and friendly to me. And didn't you say he was lean and fit, out jogging every morning?" Mrs. Abbott frowned. "He rides that bicycle like a reckless child." Her sister shrugged. "Or like an adventurous one."

Which words from the passage carry a negative connotation? Select all that apply.
o: adventurous
curious
lean
reckless
scrawny
nosy
R.w: Mrs. Abbott chooses words with negative connotations: "scrawny" (unhealthily thin), "nosy" (intrusive) and "reckless" (dangerously careless). Her sister describes the same traits with positive words.

n.0: "Adventurous" describes the same willingness to take risks as "reckless" but suggests an appealing love of excitement, a positive connotation.
n.1: "Curious" names the same interest in others as "nosy" but with a positive connotation of healthy interest.
n.2: "Lean" describes the same thin build as "scrawny" but suggests fitness, a positive connotation.

R.q:
Westbrook Clinic offered walk-in flu shots this fall for the first time, in addition to scheduled appointments. The table shows the percentage of the clinic's patients in each age group who received a flu shot at the clinic.
Age group | Last year | This year
18 to 34 | 22% | 35%
35 to 64 | 41% | 47%
65 and older | 68% | 69%
The clinic manager plans to keep walk-in hours next year.

Which conclusions are supported by the passage and table? Select all that apply.
o: More patients aged 35 to 64 got a shot this year than patients aged 65 and older.
The youngest age group showed the largest increase in its vaccination rate.
Walk-in hours caused the rise in vaccination among patients aged 18 to 34.
Older patients used the walk-in hours more often than younger patients did.
Patients 65 and older had the highest vaccination rate of the three groups this year.
The percentage of patients who got a flu shot rose in each age group this year.
R.w: Every group rose (22 to 35, 41 to 47, 68 to 69). The 18 to 34 group gained 13 points, more than 6 or 1. At 69%, patients 65 and older had the highest rate this year.

n.0: The table gives percentages, not numbers of patients; without group sizes the counts cannot be compared.
n.2: Walk-in hours began the same year, but the table shows only rates, not why they changed; causation is not established.
n.3: The table does not separate walk-in shots from scheduled ones, so use of walk-in hours by age is unknown.

R.q:
Passage 1
Protect yourself while you are here. Clean your hands before you eat, after you use the bathroom, and when you enter or leave a patient's room. Rub hand sanitizer over all surfaces of your hands until they are dry, about 20 seconds. It is okay to ask your care team, "Did you clean your hands?"

Passage 2
To: All clinical staff. Hand hygiene audits on Units 4 and 5 found compliance of 71 percent in March, below our goal of 90 percent. Beginning May 1, unit managers will post monthly audit results, and units below goal will complete a refresher module.

Which statement best describes a difference between the passages?
o: Passage 1 is written for patients and visitors; Passage 2, for hospital staff.
Passage 1 gives infection data; Passage 2 gives steps for cleaning hands.
Passage 1 is written for newly hired nurses; Passage 2, for the hospital's unit managers.
Passage 1 gives directions in the second person; Passage 2 tells a nurse's personal story.
R.w: Passage 1 speaks to "you" while you are here and invites you to ask your care team, so its audience is patients and visitors. Passage 2 is a memo addressed to all clinical staff about audit results.

n.1: This reverses the passages: Passage 1 gives the steps, and Passage 2 gives audit data.
n.2: Passage 1 invites readers to ask their care team, so it addresses patients and visitors; Passage 2 goes to all clinical staff, not just managers.
n.3: Passage 1 does address "you," but Passage 2 is a memo reporting audit data and a new policy, not a personal story.

R.q:
Tanya's four-year-old son, who weighs 36 pounds, has a fever. The pediatrician's nurse told her by phone that she may give him children's acetaminophen, but the office is now closed for the night. Tanya has a new, unopened bottle of the medicine at home and wants to be sure she gives the correct amount for his weight. She considers four sources of information.

Which source should Tanya rely on for the dose?
o: A pediatric medicine handbook from 2009 on her home bookshelf
The dosing chart printed on the label of the new bottle of medicine
A parenting forum where other parents post the doses they give
A magazine article about caring for young children with fevers
R.w: The label on the product she will actually use is specific to that medicine's strength, current, and approved for use, so it is the authoritative source for the dose.

n.0: A 2009 handbook may not match the strength of today's product; for doses, currency matters.
n.2: Forum posts are anecdotal and may involve different products, strengths, or weights.
n.3: A general magazine article is not specific to this product and is not an authoritative dosing source.

R.q:
Recipe card: Trail Mix (makes 4 servings)
Combine the entire bag of oat granola with 1 cup of mixed nuts and 1/2 cup of raisins. The nuts and raisins together contain 800 calories.

Nutrition label on the bag of granola
Serving size | 1/4 cup
Servings per container | 8
Calories per serving | 120

Jada makes the recipe exactly as written and divides it into the 4 servings the card describes.

Based on the recipe card and the label, about how many calories are in one serving of Jada's trail mix?
o: 230 calories
1,760 calories
960 calories
440 calories
R.w: Step 1: the whole bag of granola is 8 servings x 120 = 960 calories. Step 2: add the nuts and raisins: 960 + 800 = 1,760 calories, divided into 4 servings = 440 calories each.

n.0: 230 uses one label serving of granola (120 + 800 = 920, divided by 4) instead of the whole bag.
n.1: 1,760 is the total for the whole recipe, before dividing into 4 servings.
n.2: 960 is the calories in the whole bag of granola, not one serving of trail mix.

R.q:
Read the passage.

By the third week of flu season, the clinic's waiting room had become a tide that never went out. Patients filled every chair by eight in the morning, and by noon a line stretched past the pharmacy window. The receptionists stopped looking up from their screens. Dr. Patel ate lunch standing in the supply closet, and the nurses traded their usual jokes for quick nods. Still, every patient who came through the door was seen before the clinic closed, even when that meant locking up after nine at night.

The phrase "a tide that never went out" suggests that the waiting room
o: stayed full as new patients kept arriving throughout the day
emptied each afternoon after the busy morning rush ended
was busiest during the hours after the clinic had closed
was flooded during a storm that delayed patients' visits
R.w: A tide that never goes out stays high. The details that follow (chairs full by eight, a line by noon, staff working past nine) confirm the room stayed crowded as patients kept coming all day.

n.1: Opposite of the metaphor: the tide never went out, and the line grew by noon.
n.2: Misreads the detail about locking up late, which shows staff stayed to finish, not that the room was busiest after closing.
n.3: Takes the metaphor literally; nothing in the passage describes water or a storm.

R.q:
Since the new staffing rules took effect, each nurse on our unit has cared for no more than five patients per shift, down from seven. I finally have time to explain a new medication properly, to notice when a patient's breathing changes, and to eat lunch sitting down. Management keeps talking about the cost of hiring more staff. They are not the ones running between rooms at 3 a.m. when two call lights go off at once.

The author of the passage is most likely
o: a reporter writing a news story about staffing rules.
a hospital administrator reviewing the cost of new staff.
a patient who was recently treated on the unit.
a nurse who works shifts on the unit.
R.w: The author refers to "our unit," describes caring for patients and explaining medications, and contrasts the writer's own night-shift experience with management's view. These details point to a staff nurse's perspective.

n.0: A news reporter would write in a neutral voice, but this author writes from personal, first-hand experience.
n.1: The author criticizes management for focusing on cost, which is the opposite of an administrator's perspective.
n.2: The author describes caring for several patients at once, which a patient would not do.

R.q:
Read the instructions.

Patient Registration Form: Instructions
Section A: All patients complete.
Section B: Complete if you have health insurance. If you are covered by more than one plan, list the primary plan first.
Section C: Complete if the patient is under 18; a parent or legal guardian must sign.
Section D: Complete if you are applying for the clinic's sliding-fee discount. Attach a recent pay stub or tax return.
Section E: All patients sign and date.

Luis is 34 years old. He has no health insurance, and he is applying for the clinic's sliding-fee discount.

Which sections should Luis complete?
o: Sections A, D and E
Sections A and E, and attach a pay stub
Sections A, B, D and E
Sections A, C, D and E
R.w: Every patient completes A and E. Section D applies because Luis is applying for the discount. Section B applies to insured patients and Section C to patients under 18, and neither describes Luis.

n.1: The pay stub goes with Section D, which Luis must also complete.
n.2: Section B is for patients with insurance, and Luis has none.
n.3: Section C is for patients under 18, and Luis is 34.

R.q:
Passage 1
From a beverage industry statement: A standard can of our energy drink contains about the same amount of caffeine as a large cup of coffee. Parents who are comfortable with their teenagers drinking coffee should have no greater concern about energy drinks.

Passage 2
From a pediatrician: A single can may hold about as much caffeine as coffee, but teenagers rarely sip energy drinks slowly the way they sip hot coffee. Many drink two or three cans quickly, often during sports, and some mix them with other caffeinated products. That pattern, not the single can, is what sends teens to emergency rooms with racing hearts.

How would the author of Passage 2 most likely respond to the claim in Passage 1?
o: The comparison ignores how quickly and in what amounts teens drink them.
Teens who drink coffee face the same risks as those who drink energy drinks.
Energy drinks contain much more caffeine per can than coffee does.
The industry is correct, so parents can set aside their concerns.
R.w: The pediatrician grants that one can is similar to coffee but argues that the real danger is drinking several cans quickly. That response targets the industry's single-can comparison.

n.1: The pediatrician contrasts how teens drink coffee and energy drinks, so the risks are not presented as the same.
n.2: The pediatrician concedes that a can may hold about as much caffeine as coffee.
n.3: The pediatrician describes emergency room visits, which shows continued concern.

R.q:
A new study reports that adults who took VitaCore daily for 12 weeks had 30 percent fewer sick days than adults who took a placebo, or sugar pill. The study included 64 office workers in one city. It was paid for and run by VitaCore Nutrition, the company that sells the supplement, and its results have not been reviewed by outside scientists. VitaCore's website now calls the product "clinically proven to keep you healthy all year."

Which detail from the passage most strongly suggests that the study's findings may be biased?
o: The study compared the supplement with a placebo.
The study reported its main result as a percentage of sick days.
The study included 64 office workers from one city.
The supplement's seller paid for and ran the study.
R.w: A company that profits from the product has a financial interest in a favorable result. When the seller funds and runs its own study, the findings may be slanted toward the product, which is a classic source of bias.

n.0: A placebo comparison is a strength of study design; it helps rule out the effect of simply taking a pill.
n.1: Reporting a result as a percentage is a neutral way to present data and says nothing about whose interests the study serves.
n.2: A small, local sample makes the evidence less sufficient and harder to generalize, but that is a limitation of size, not a sign that the results were slanted toward one side.

R.q:
For three years, Priya and Elena had finished first and second at the county science fair, always in that order. This spring, Priya's solar oven cracked the night before judging. At ten o'clock, Elena knocked on her door with a roll of foil, a glue gun, and her own notes on insulation. They worked until midnight. The next day Elena took first place, and Priya took third. Walking out of the gym, Priya expected to feel crushed. Instead, she found herself planning next year's project with Elena, and the ribbon in her pocket felt lighter than she had expected.

Which statement best expresses the theme of the passage?
o: Kindness from a rival can turn a competition into a friendship.
The long rivalry between two students at a county science fair
Elena helps Priya repair her solar oven on the night before the science fair.
Hard work is the surest path to winning first place in a contest.
R.w: A theme is a message about life stated as a complete idea. Elena's help changes Priya's feelings about losing and leads to shared plans, so the story's message is that a rival's kindness can build friendship.

n.1: This names the topic of the story in a phrase; it does not state a message about it.
n.2: This is a plot summary of one event, not the message the story conveys.
n.3: Priya worked hard yet placed third; the story's focus is the friendship, not a recipe for winning.

R.q:
Read the passage.

At Juniper Elementary, the school garden began as four raised beds behind the gym. Third graders now plant lettuce, carrots and peas each spring, and the cafeteria serves the harvest at a salad bar one week each May. Teacher Rosa Lin, who started the garden, says that students who once refused anything green now ask for second helpings of the salad they grew. Last year, the parent group raised money to add eight more beds and a rain barrel. The principal has asked other teachers whether they would like to use the garden for science lessons.

Which statements are supported by the passage? Select all that apply.
o: The cafeteria serves vegetables from the garden throughout the spring.
Several other teachers now use the garden for their science lessons.
The garden has grown larger since it was first started.
The principal is interested in expanding how the garden is used.
The parent group paid for the original four raised beds.
According to Ms. Lin, some students eat more vegetables they grew.
R.w: The garden went from four beds to twelve. Ms. Lin reports students asking for seconds of the salad they grew. The principal asking other teachers about science lessons shows interest in wider use.

n.0: Distortion: the harvest is served at a salad bar one week each May, not throughout the spring.
n.1: Goes beyond the passage: the principal has asked teachers whether they would like to use it; nothing says any of them do yet.
n.4: Wrong detail: the parent group paid for the eight added beds and a rain barrel, not the original four.

R.q:
The town of Brookfield added a Route 9 bus to its east side three years ago. The table shows average riders per weekday.
Year | Route 9 riders | All routes combined
Year 1 | 420 | 5,100
Year 2 | 610 | 5,350
Year 3 | 800 | 5,560
A town report says Route 9's growth came mostly from new apartment buildings along its path. Two more buildings on the route are scheduled to open next year, and no other changes to bus service are planned.

Which prediction is best supported by the passage and table?
o: Route 9 ridership will most likely keep rising next year as the new buildings open.
Route 9 will carry more riders next year than all of the other routes put together.
Ridership on all routes combined will climb to about 8,000 riders per weekday next year.
Riders from other routes will likely switch to Route 9, lowering ridership on those routes.
R.w: Route 9 grew by about 190 riders a year, the report ties that growth to new apartment buildings on the route, and two more buildings open next year. The cause is still in motion, so continued growth is the supported prediction.

n.1: The other routes carry about 4,760 riders; Route 9 would need to grow sixfold in one year to pass them.
n.2: Combined ridership grew by about 200 to 250 a year; a jump of about 2,400 over-extends the trend.
n.3: Ridership on the other routes rose slightly each year (4,680, 4,740, 4,760), so the trend does not show riders leaving them.

R.q:
From Lakeview Hospital's sustainability report: Since switching to reusable surgical gowns, the hospital has cut its gown waste by 1,200 pounds per month. (The report counts a month as four weeks.) The reusable gowns are laundered on site and replaced after about 75 uses.
Chart: Hospital waste by category, after the switch (pounds per week)
Packaging | 900
Food | 1,400
Surgical gowns | 150
Other | 600

Based on the report and the chart, about how many pounds of gown waste did the hospital produce per week before the switch?
o: 300 pounds
450 pounds
1,050 pounds
1,350 pounds
R.w: Step 1: convert the report's monthly cut to weekly: 1,200 / 4 = 300 pounds per week. Step 2: add it to the chart's weekly figure after the switch: 150 + 300 = 450 pounds per week before.

n.0: 300 pounds is the weekly reduction, not the weekly amount before the switch.
n.2: 1,050 subtracts the weekly figure from the monthly cut (1,200 - 150), mixing units and reversing the direction.
n.3: 1,350 adds the monthly cut to a weekly figure (1,200 + 150) without converting units.

R.q:
Read the directions and the description.

Mixing Powdered Infant Formula
1. Wash your hands and clean the work area.
2. Boil fresh water, then let it cool for no more than 30 minutes.
3. Pour the water into a clean bottle first, then add the powder.
4. Use the scoop from the can and level each scoop with a clean knife. Add one level scoop for every 2 fluid ounces of water.
5. Cap the bottle and shake until the powder dissolves.
6. Cool the bottle under running water, and test a few drops on your inner wrist before feeding.

After washing his hands and wiping the counter, Terrell boiled fresh water and let it cool for 20 minutes. He put three heaping scoops of powder into a clean bottle, poured in 6 fluid ounces of the water, and shook the bottle until the powder dissolved. He cooled the bottle under running water and tested a few drops on his wrist.

Which directions did Terrell fail to follow? Select all that apply.
o: Use one scoop of powder for every 2 fluid ounces of water
Test a few drops on the inner wrist before feeding
Pour the water into the bottle before adding the powder
Level each scoop of powder with a clean knife
Let the boiled water cool for no more than 30 minutes
R.w: Terrell put the powder in before the water (step 3 says water first) and used heaping scoops instead of level ones (step 4). He followed the other directions.

n.0: Three scoops for 6 fluid ounces is the correct ratio of one scoop per 2 ounces; the error was that the scoops were heaping.
n.1: He tested a few drops on his wrist, as directed.
n.4: He let the water cool for 20 minutes, within the 30-minute limit.

R.q:
Why do so many water mains break in January? Water expands by about 9 percent when it freezes. When the ground around a buried pipe freezes, it shifts and pushes against the pipe, placing stress on joints and older sections. Cold water inside the pipe also makes metal and plastic more brittle. As a result, a pipe that has handled years of normal pressure can crack during a hard freeze. Older cast-iron mains are especially likely to fail because decades of corrosion have already thinned their walls.

Which organizational structure does the author mainly use?
o: problem and solution
chronological order
classification
cause and effect
R.w: The passage opens with a "why" question and answers it with causes (freezing, shifting ground, brittleness, corrosion) and their effect (cracked pipes). Signal words such as "as a result" and "because" confirm a cause-and-effect structure.

n.0: The passage explains the breaks but proposes no fix, so it lacks the solution half of this structure.
n.1: The passage explains why something happens, not a series of events in time order.
n.2: Cast-iron mains are singled out once, but the passage does not sort pipes into categories.

R.q:
Read the table.

Flu Vaccination Rates by Age Group, Pinewood Clinic Patients
Age group | 2023 | 2024 | 2025
18 to 34 | 31% | 34% | 38%
35 to 49 | 40% | 39% | 43%
50 to 64 | 52% | 55% | 54%
65 and older | 68% | 70% | 74%
Rates show the percentage of clinic patients in each age group who received a flu vaccine during the season.

Which statements are supported by the table? Select all that apply.
o: The 50-to-64 group's rate fell slightly from 2024 to 2025.
The 65-and-older group had the highest rate in every year shown.
The 35-to-49 group's rate rose each year from 2023 to 2025.
The 18-to-34 group's rate will pass 50 percent by the year 2028.
The 18-to-34 group's rate rose each year from 2023 to 2025.
More patients age 65 and older were vaccinated than patients 18 to 34.
R.w: The 65-and-older row is highest in each column (68%, 70%, 74%). The 18-to-34 row rises 31%, 34%, 38%. The 50-to-64 row drops from 55% to 54% between 2024 and 2025.

n.2: The 35-to-49 rate dipped from 40% to 39% in 2024 before rising.
n.3: Extrapolates beyond the table, which shows data only through 2025.
n.5: The table gives percentages within each group, not numbers of patients, so counts cannot be compared.

R.q:
From a nurses' council proposal: Night-shift nurses on our medical units often skip their meal breaks to keep up with patient call lights. Fatigue and hunger make it harder to concentrate during the early morning medication pass. We propose that every night-shift nurse take a protected, uninterrupted 30-minute meal break, with a float nurse covering patients. We believe this change will reduce medication errors on night shift.

Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the proposal's argument?
o: Many nurses say that the meal break is the most welcome part of a long night shift.
On a unit that tested protected breaks, night-shift medication errors fell by a fifth.
Medication errors are reported more often on night shifts than on day shifts.
Night-shift nurses who take uninterrupted breaks will make fewer errors with medications.
R.w: A trial showing fewer night-shift errors after protected breaks were introduced is new evidence that links the proposed change to the predicted result.

n.0: Nurses' liking for breaks says nothing about medication errors.
n.2: This shows that night errors are a problem but not that protected breaks would reduce them.
n.3: This simply restates the proposal's conclusion; repeating a claim does not add support for it.

R.q:
The research team had spent four months collecting blood samples from 200 volunteers. Then, during a power outage, the freezer that stored the samples failed overnight, and every sample was ruined. When the lead researcher, Dr. Kim, called the team together the next morning, she admitted that they were back to square one. Within a week, the team had begun recruiting new volunteers.

As used in the passage, the phrase "back to square one" means that the team was
o: returned to its original laboratory.
forced to start the work over.
waiting for the power to return.
blamed for losing the samples.
R.w: The idiom means having to start again from the beginning. The ruined samples and the team's decision to recruit new volunteers confirm that the work had to restart.

n.0: This reads the idiom literally as a place; the passage never mentions the team moving anywhere.
n.2: The outage had already happened; the idiom describes the loss of progress, not a wait for power.
n.3: No one is blamed; the freezer failed during a power outage.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Dr. Mae Chen is best known for the community clinic she opened in Oakland in 1998, but her path there was not direct. She had first trained as a pharmacist, graduating in 1979. After six years at a hospital pharmacy, she entered medical school in 1985, the same year her daughter was born. She completed her residency in family medicine in 1992 and spent the next six years at a rural clinic in Nevada before returning to the Bay Area. Today the Oakland clinic serves more than 9,000 patients a year.

Place the events in Dr. Chen's career in the order in which they occurred, starting with the earliest.
o: She completes her residency in family medicine
She opens the community clinic in Oakland
She graduates as a pharmacist
She works at a rural clinic in Nevada
She enters medical school
R.w: Pharmacy graduation (1979), medical school (1985), residency completed (1992), six years in Nevada (1992 to 1998), then the Oakland clinic (1998). The passage mentions the clinic first, but it happened last.

R.q:
Most vaccines must be kept between 36 and 46 degrees Fahrenheit from the moment they leave the factory until they are given to a patient. This unbroken chain of refrigeration is called the cold chain. Vaccines travel in insulated containers with temperature monitors, and clinics store them in refrigerators that record the temperature every few minutes. If a reading falls outside the safe range, staff label the vaccines "do not use" and contact the state health department, which decides whether the doses can still be given.

What is the primary purpose of the passage?
o: to persuade readers to receive recommended vaccines
to explain how vaccines are kept safely cold
to criticize clinics that store vaccines incorrectly
to describe the history of vaccine refrigeration
R.w: The passage defines the cold chain and walks through how vaccines are shipped, stored, monitored and handled when a problem occurs. Its neutral, step-by-step explanation shows an informative purpose.

n.0: The topic is vaccines, but the passage never urges anyone to be vaccinated. Confusing the topic with the purpose leads to this choice.
n.2: The passage describes what staff do when temperatures go out of range; it does not fault any clinic.
n.3: No dates or past developments are given; the passage describes current practice.

R.q:
In a television commercial, a famous Olympic swimmer holds up a bottle of DreamEase, a sleep supplement. "I have won six gold medals," she says, "and I trust DreamEase to help me sleep before every race. If it works for a champion, it will work for you." The commercial shows her diving into a pool as the product name appears on screen. It does not mention any research on the supplement or its ingredients.

Which statement best describes the main weakness of the commercial's argument?
o: It criticizes rival supplements instead of describing its own product.
It claims the product works because many people already use it.
It presents two choices for better sleep when many others are available.
It relies on a celebrity whose expertise has no bearing on the product.
R.w: The swimmer's medals show athletic skill, not knowledge of sleep or supplements, and no research is offered. Using an irrelevant authority as proof is an appeal to false authority.

n.0: No rival products are mentioned.
n.1: The commercial relies on one famous person, not on how many people use the product, so it is not a bandwagon appeal.
n.2: The commercial does not frame a choice between two options.

R.q:
For a history project on nurses in World War I, Paige wants to explain how Lena Harlow, an American army nurse, felt about working near the front lines in France. Her teacher has asked students to present the nurse's own words and feelings rather than someone else's account of them. The school library has several items about Harlow and about nursing in the war.

Which source would best meet Paige's purpose?
o: A collection of the letters Harlow wrote home from France
A textbook chapter on the role of nurses in World War I
A biography of Harlow written in 1985 by her grand-niece
An encyclopedia entry that summarizes Harlow's nursing career
R.w: Letters Harlow wrote from France are a primary source in her own words, recorded at the time, which is exactly what the assignment asks for.

n.1: A textbook chapter describes nurses in general and is secondary.
n.2: Even a family member's biography is a secondary account that interprets Harlow's experience.
n.3: An encyclopedia entry is a tertiary summary, not Harlow's own words.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Last summer, the town of Mesa Verde faced its driest season in forty years, and its reservoir fell to 30 percent of capacity. The water district asked residents to cut their use by one fifth.

The district paired the request with practical help. It offered rebates of up to $500 for replacing lawns with native plants, gave away low-flow showerheads, and posted each neighborhood's weekly water use on its website. Mayor Tina Okafor, who had replaced her own lawn with cactus and gravel, appeared in a video about the rebates.

By September, total water use had fallen 23 percent from the year before. District officials credit the neighborhood reports most of all, saying residents responded when they could compare their use with their neighbors'.

Which statements belong in a summary of the passage? Select all that apply.
o: Other towns facing a severe drought should post each neighborhood's weekly water use online.
Water use fell 23 percent, a drop officials credit mainly to the neighborhood reports.
Residents cut back mainly because $500 rebates covered the full cost of replacing a lawn.
During a severe drought, the water district asked residents to cut their use by one fifth.
Mayor Tina Okafor replaced her own lawn with cactus and gravel before appearing in a rebate video.
The district backed its request with rebates, free fixtures and neighborhood use reports.
R.w: A summary keeps each paragraph's key point in order: the drought and the request (paragraph 1), the district's support measures (paragraph 2), and the result with the officials' explanation (paragraph 3).

n.0: This is a recommendation the passage never makes; a summary adds no opinions.
n.2: Distortion: rebates were up to $500, the passage never says they covered the full cost, and officials credit the reports, not the rebates, most.
n.4: The mayor's own lawn is a minor detail; a summary leaves out such details.

R.q:
Greenway Pharmacy opened a drive-through window in June. The manager tracked the average wait from a customer's arrival to pickup.
Month | Counter wait | Drive-through wait
May | 14 min | not open
June | 11 min | 6 min
July | 10 min | 9 min
August | 10 min | 12 min
The manager noted that drive-through use grew each month as word spread, while one employee continued to staff the window.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage and table?
o: As use of the drive-through grew, its wait became longer than the wait at the counter.
Opening the drive-through cut the counter wait by 4 minutes in each month after May.
Customers prefer the counter to the drive-through because the counter wait is shorter.
Adding a second employee at the window would bring the drive-through wait back to 6 minutes.
R.w: Drive-through use grew every month with one employee, and its wait rose from 6 to 9 to 12 minutes. By August it was longer than the 10-minute counter wait.

n.1: The counter wait fell by 3 minutes in June (14 to 11) and by 4 in July and August, so it did not drop by 4 in each month.
n.2: The passage says drive-through use grew each month, which does not suggest customers prefer the counter.
n.3: This is a prediction the data cannot test; staffing never changed, so the effect of a second employee is unknown.

R.q:
Read the description of the line graph.

Title: Average Daily Steps of Walking Club Members, Weeks 1 to 6
Vertical axis: Average steps per day
Horizontal axis: Week of the program
Plotted points:
Week 1: 4,200
Week 2: 5,100
Week 3: 5,900
Week 4: 6,400
Week 5: 6,500
Week 6: 6,550
The points are joined by a single line. The club meets three times a week at a city park.

Which statement is best supported by the graph?
o: Average steps rose quickly in the early weeks and then leveled off.
Average steps rose by about the same amount each week of the program.
Members will be averaging more than 8,000 steps a day by week 10.
Members walked fewer steps per day in week 6 than they did in week 4.
R.w: The weekly gains were 900, 800, 500, 100 and 50 steps. Large early increases followed by very small ones mean the line climbs steeply and then flattens.

n.1: The gains shrank from 900 steps to 50 steps, so they were not equal.
n.2: Extrapolates beyond the graph, and the shrinking gains suggest the trend is leveling off, not continuing upward.
n.3: Week 6 (6,550) is higher than week 4 (6,400).

R.q:
Hospitals today spend millions of dollars on hand-hygiene programs, yet studies still find that health care workers clean their hands less than half as often as they should. The idea itself is not new. In 1847, a Hungarian doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis required doctors at a Vienna maternity clinic to wash their hands in a chlorine solution before examining patients, and deaths among new mothers in his ward fell sharply. The challenge today is not knowledge but habit: busy staff forget, skip steps or assume gloves are enough.

The author mentions Ignaz Semmelweis mainly to
o: show that the value of handwashing has been known for a long time.
entertain readers with a story about a famous European doctor.
explain how chlorine solutions kill the germs that cause infection.
persuade readers that modern doctors should study medical history.
R.w: The sentence just before the example says "The idea itself is not new," and the Semmelweis example from 1847 supports that point. The detail sets up the author's argument that today's problem is habit, not lack of knowledge.

n.1: The example is brief and factual; it serves the author's point about habit rather than amusing the reader.
n.2: The passage says Semmelweis used chlorine but never explains how it works on germs.
n.3: The author never suggests that doctors study history; the example supports a point about hand hygiene.

R.q:
Standing desks have become common in American offices. A 2019 study of 300 office workers found that those who used standing desks for six months reported less lower-back pain than those who did not. Standing desks cost between $250 and $700 at major office suppliers. Several workers in the study said they felt more alert in the afternoon. It is a well-established fact that a standing desk is the healthiest choice for any office.

Which of the following statements is an opinion, even though the author presents it as established?
o: Standing desks cost between $250 and $700 at major office suppliers.
Workers who used standing desks for six months reported less lower-back pain.
Several workers in the study said they felt more alert in the afternoon.
A standing desk is the healthiest choice for any office.
R.w: Calling something "the healthiest choice for any office" is a sweeping judgment. Labeling it "a well-established fact" does not make it one; the study supports a narrower finding about back pain, not a ranking of every option for every office.

n.0: Prices can be verified at the suppliers, so this is a fact.
n.1: This reports a study result that can be checked against the published study, so it is a fact.
n.2: "Felt more alert" describes a feeling, but the statement reports what workers said, which the study records can confirm. It is a fact about their reports.

R.q:
The Millbrook City Council voted 5 to 2 in June to spend $1.2 million on the River Walk Trail. Construction crews began clearing the route along the riverbank in August. When finished, the paved trail will be 3.4 miles long, according to the approved plans. Council member Dana Whitfield, who voted yes, told reporters, "This trail will draw thousands of new visitors and bring our downtown shops back to life."

Which of the following statements from the article is an opinion?
o: The trail will draw thousands of new visitors and revive downtown shops.
The approved plans call for a paved trail 3.4 miles long.
Construction crews began clearing the route along the riverbank in August.
The council voted 5 to 2 in June to spend $1.2 million on the River Walk Trail.
R.w: Whitfield is predicting future results and judging their effect on downtown. A prediction like this cannot be proven when it is made, and others may expect different results, so it is an opinion.

n.1: The planned length is written in the approved documents and can be checked now, so this is a fact about the plan, not a guess about the future.
n.2: The start of construction can be confirmed by records or observation, so this is a fact.
n.3: The vote count and amount are part of the public council record, so they are facts.

R.q:
Read the label.

Drug Facts
Active ingredient (in each tablet): Ibuprofen 200 mg. Purpose: pain reliever and fever reducer.
Uses: temporarily relieves minor aches and pains due to headache, toothache, backache, menstrual cramps, the common cold and muscle aches; temporarily reduces fever.
Directions: Adults and children 12 years and over: take 1 tablet every 4 to 6 hours while symptoms last. If pain or fever does not respond to 1 tablet, 2 tablets may be used. Do not take more than 6 tablets in 24 hours unless a doctor directs you to. Children under 12: ask a doctor.
Stop use and ask a doctor if: pain gets worse or lasts more than 10 days; fever gets worse or lasts more than 3 days.

According to the label, when should an adult stop using the product and ask a doctor?
o: When more than 2 tablets are needed in a day
When a fever has lasted for more than 3 days
When one tablet does not relieve the pain
When pain has lasted for more than 3 days
R.w: The "Stop use and ask a doctor if" section lists a fever that gets worse or lasts more than 3 days.

n.0: The daily limit is 6 tablets in 24 hours, so needing more than 2 is within the directions.
n.2: If 1 tablet does not work, the directions allow 2 tablets; this is not a reason to stop.
n.3: Mixes up the limits: the label allows pain to last up to 10 days before asking a doctor; 3 days is the fever limit.

R.q:
Read the passage.

In the Del Rio water district, the average resident uses about 92 gallons of water a day at home in summer and about 58 gallons a day in winter. The difference comes mostly from lawn watering, which makes up about 40 percent of summer use but only about 5 percent of winter use. Indoor use changes little across the year. Toilets account for the most indoor water, about 18 gallons per person per day, followed by showers at about 13 gallons and faucets at about 11. Replacing an older toilet with a high-efficiency model saves about 9 gallons per person per day.

According to the passage, which statement about winter water use in Del Rio is accurate?
o: Toilets use noticeably less water than they do in the summer months.
Lawn watering makes up about 40 percent of a resident's home use.
The average resident uses about 58 gallons of water a day at home.
Showers account for about 18 gallons per person per day indoors.
R.w: The first sentence gives winter home use as about 58 gallons a day for the average resident.

n.0: Contradicted: the passage says indoor use changes little across the year.
n.1: 40 percent is the summer share; lawn watering is about 5 percent of winter use.
n.3: 18 gallons is the figure for toilets; showers use about 13 gallons.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Rosa had worked at the corner bakery for three years by the time she enrolled in night classes at the community college. She kept her weekday job until she finished her prerequisites, then switched to weekend shifts when her clinical rotations began. Those two years were the hardest of her life. She passed her licensing exam the summer after graduation and started at County General that fall, but she still stops by the bakery every Saturday for a cinnamon roll.

According to the passage, which event happened immediately after Rosa finished her prerequisites?
o: She passed her nursing licensing exam.
She started working at County General.
She enrolled in night classes at the college.
She switched to weekend shifts at the bakery.
R.w: Rosa kept her weekday job "until she finished her prerequisites, then switched to weekend shifts" when clinical rotations began. The signal word "then" marks the next event.

n.0: The licensing exam came the summer after graduation, well after the switch to weekends.
n.1: She started at County General in the fall after passing her exam, the last event.
n.2: She enrolled in night classes before taking her prerequisites.

R.q:
Read the passage.

In the 1840s, a Vienna hospital ran two maternity wards. In one, women were delivered by doctors and medical students; in the other, by midwives. Mothers in the doctors' ward died of fever far more often, and some women begged to be admitted to the midwives' ward instead. The physician Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that the doctors often came straight from performing autopsies. When he required them to wash their hands in a chlorine solution before examining patients, deaths in their ward fell sharply. Many of his colleagues rejected his findings, partly because germs had not yet been identified as a cause of disease.

Why does the author most likely mention that some women begged to be admitted to the midwives' ward?
o: To suggest that the midwives in Vienna were better trained than the doctors
To explain why Semmelweis began requiring the doctors to wash their hands
To illustrate why Semmelweis's colleagues rejected his findings about fever
To show that the gap in death rates was so large that even patients knew of it
R.w: The detail comes right after the statement that mothers in the doctors' ward died far more often. Women pleading to avoid that ward shows the difference was obvious and well known, which makes the problem vivid for the reader.

n.0: The passage never compares training; it links the deaths to doctors coming from autopsies.
n.1: The handwashing rule is explained by the autopsy observation, not by the women's requests.
n.2: Wrong part of the passage: the colleagues' rejection is explained by germs not yet being identified.

R.q:
Every evening, Mr. Okafor walked the length of his garden and studied the sky over the western ridge. The farmers in the valley joked that he trusted clouds more than the radio. That afternoon, the radio had promised a dry night. But as he finished his walk, he watched the swallows skim low over the field and felt the first cool gust that, in his experience, came about an hour before a storm. He stood still for a long moment, then turned toward the shed where he kept the canvas covers.

What will Mr. Okafor most likely do next?
o: Leave his plants uncovered because the radio predicted a dry night.
Ask the valley farmers whether they also expect a storm tonight.
Cover his plants because he expects a storm despite the forecast.
Harvest his ripest vegetables before a hard frost arrives tonight.
R.w: The passage says he trusts the sky over the radio, he notices the gust that usually comes before a storm, and he heads for the shed with the canvas covers. All point to covering his plants.

n.0: He turns toward the canvas covers, and he is known to trust the sky over the radio, so he is unlikely to rely on the forecast.
n.1: Nothing suggests he will consult anyone; he trusts his own reading of the sky and is already heading to the shed.
n.3: The signs he notices point to a storm; the passage mentions no cold or frost.

R.q:
A district analysis found that the high schools with the most vending machines also had the lowest average test scores. At the next meeting, a board member said, "Vending machines are hurting our students' learning. If we remove them, test scores will rise." The same analysis showed that the schools with more vending machines were also larger and had fewer counselors per student, but the board member did not mention those findings.

Which statement best describes the flaw in the board member's reasoning?
o: It bases a broad conclusion on the experience of a single high school.
It rejects the district's analysis because of the people who wrote it.
It predicts that one small change will lead to a series of disasters.
It treats a link between two things as proof that one causes the other.
R.w: Vending machines and low scores occur together, but the board member assumes the machines cause the scores, even though school size and counselor numbers also differ. That treats correlation as causation.

n.0: The analysis covered several high schools, so the problem is not a single example.
n.1: The board member uses the analysis rather than rejecting it, and no one is attacked.
n.2: The board member predicts a benefit from one change, not a chain of disasters.

M.q: A bottle contains 15 tablets. Each prescribed dose is 3/4 of a tablet, and tablets are scored so they can be split. How many doses does the bottle contain?
M.w: Divide the supply by the dose: 15 ÷ 3/4 = 15 × 4/3 = 60/3 = 20 doses.

n.0: 11 1/4 is 15 × 3/4, the multiplication instead of the division.
n.2: 5 divides 15 by the numerator 3 and ignores the denominator 4.
n.3: 60 multiplies by 4 but does not then divide by 3.

M.q: During a quality check, 5 out of every 16 IV bags sampled had a label printed off-center. What percent of the sampled bags had an off-center label? Enter the number only, without the percent sign.

tr.3.125: Moved the decimal point only 1 place right.
tr.0.3125: Left the answer as a decimal instead of converting to a percent.

M.w: 5/16 = 5 ÷ 16 = 0.3125. Multiply by 100 to write it as a percent: 0.3125 × 100 = 31.25, so 31.25%.

M.q: A stacked bar graph shows clinic visits by age group. The April bar reaches 240 visits in total. Its 'Under 18' segment runs from 0 to 70, its '18 to 64' segment from 70 to 185, and its '65 and older' segment from 185 to 240. To the nearest tenth of a percent, what percent of April visits were by patients aged 18 to 64?
M.w: A middle segment's value is its top minus its bottom: 185 - 70 = 115 visits. 115 / 240 = 0.4792, or 47.9%.

n.1: 185 / 240 = 77.1% reads the top edge of the segment (185) as its value instead of subtracting the 70 below it.
n.2: 55 / 240 = 22.9% is the '65 and older' segment (240 - 185).
n.3: 70 / 240 = 29.2% is the 'Under 18' segment.

M.q: A student is checking which expressions are equivalent to 3(2x - 4) + 2x. Select all that apply.
M.w: Simplify: 3(2x - 4) + 2x = 6x - 12 + 2x = 8x - 12. Check the factored forms: 4(2x - 3) = 8x - 12 and 2(4x - 6) = 8x - 12, so both are equivalent.

n.2: This equals 5(2x - 4), as if the 2x outside the parentheses were added to the 3. The 2x is a separate term, not part of the multiplier.
n.3: Sign error: 3 × (-4) = -12, not +12.
n.5: This distributes the 3 to 2x but not to -4. 3(2x - 4) = 6x - 12, so the constant is -12.

M.q: A student checks the work on a practice set. What value of x makes the equation 5x - 9 = 26 true?
M.w: Add 9 to both sides: 5x = 35. Divide both sides by 5: x = 7. Check: 5(7) - 9 = 35 - 9 = 26.

n.0: This divides 26 by 5 but leaves the -9 undivided, giving x - 9 = 5.2. Move the 9 first, then divide.
n.1: Sign error: 9 was subtracted from 26 instead of added, giving 5x = 17.
n.2: This stops after adding 9 to both sides; 5x = 35 still has to be divided by 5.

M.q: A lawn sprinkler waters a circular region with an area of 113.04 square meters. A landscaper needs the width of the region measured straight across through its center. What is the diameter of the watered region? Use 3.14 for pi.
o: 6 m

n.0: 6 m is the radius; the diameter is twice the radius.
n.2: This divides the area by 2π (6.28), as if A = 2πr.
n.3: 36 is r²; take its square root to find r, then double it.

M.q: Four patients' meal trays were checked after lunch. Ana ate 5/8 of her meal, Ben ate 0.63 of his, Carmen ate 61% of hers and Dev ate 3/5 of his. Who ate the greatest portion?
o: Ana
Carmen
Dev
Ben
M.w: Convert to decimals: Ana 5/8 = 0.625, Ben 0.63 = 0.630, Carmen 61% = 0.61, Dev 3/5 = 0.6. The greatest is 0.630, so Ben ate the most.

n.0: 5/8 = 0.625, which is slightly less than 0.630.
n.1: 61% = 0.61, which is less than 0.625 and 0.63.
n.2: 3/5 = 0.6, the least of the four portions.

M.q: In a nursing course, exams count for 50% of the final grade, quizzes for 30%, and homework for 20%. Priya's averages are 82 on exams, 90 on quizzes, and 95 on homework. What is Priya's final course grade? Enter the number only.
A lab technician records a reagent concentration as 0.045. Which list contains three values that are each equivalent to 0.045?
M.w: 0.045 × 100 = 4.5%. As a fraction, 0.045 has three decimal places: 45/1,000. Dividing both terms by 5 gives 9/200. All three values in that list equal 0.045.

n.1: Every value in this list equals 0.45, ten times 0.045.
n.2: 4.5% and 45/1,000 are correct, but 9/20 = 0.45, so the list fails.
n.3: Every value in this list equals 0.0045, one tenth of 0.045.

M.q: A medical assistant's hourly wage rose from $18.40 to $20.70. What was the percent increase in the hourly wage? Enter the number only, without the percent sign.

tr.11.11: Divided the $2.30 raise by the new wage, $20.70, instead of the original wage.
tr.2.3: Reported the dollar increase instead of the percent increase.

M.q: Four lab measurements are recorded as 1.105, 1 1/8, 1.09 and 112%. Place the measurements in order from greatest to least, starting with the greatest.

In a hospital volunteer program, the ratio of high school volunteers to college volunteers is 3:5, and there are 40 volunteers in total. How many more high school volunteers must join so that the ratio becomes 1:1?
M.w: Total parts = 3 + 5 = 8, so each part = 40 ÷ 8 = 5. High school: 3 × 5 = 15; college: 5 × 5 = 25. For 1:1, the high school group needs 25, so 25 - 15 = 10 must join.

n.1: This subtracts the ratio terms (5 - 3). The actual groups are 15 and 25 volunteers.
n.2: This is the current number of high school volunteers, not the number who must join.
n.3: This is the number of college volunteers, which is the target size of the high school group, not the number who must join.

M.q: A box plot of waiting times, in minutes, at a walk-in clinic shows a minimum of 4, a first quartile of 11, a median of 18, a third quartile of 27, and a maximum of 52. Which statement is supported by the plot?
o: About 25% of the patients waited over 18 minutes
About half the waits were 11 to 27 minutes
The interquartile range was 48 minutes
The mean waiting time was 18 minutes
M.w: The box runs from Q1 (11) to Q3 (27) and holds the middle 50% of the data, so about half the waits were between 11 and 27 minutes.

n.0: About 50% of the values lie above the median of 18, not 25%.
n.2: 52 - 4 = 48 is the range. The IQR is 27 - 11 = 16 minutes.
n.3: 18 is the median; a box plot does not show the mean.

M.q: A home health nurse drives 30 miles to a patient's home at an average of 60 miles per hour and returns along the same route at an average of 40 miles per hour. What is her average speed for the whole round trip?
o: 48 miles per hour
40 miles per hour
24 miles per hour
50 miles per hour
M.w: Time out: 30 ÷ 60 = 0.5 hour. Time back: 30 ÷ 40 = 0.75 hour. Total: 60 miles in 1.25 hours, so 60 ÷ 1.25 = 48 miles per hour.

n.1: This uses the slower return speed as if it applied to the whole trip.
n.2: This divides the one-way distance of 30 miles by the total time of 1.25 hours.
n.3: This averages the two speeds. Average speed is total distance ÷ total time, and more time is spent at the slower speed.

M.q: A patient is prescribed 1.5 tablets three times a day. The pharmacy dispenses 90 tablets. How many full days will the supply last?
o: 20 days
60 days
135 days
30 days
M.w: Tablets per day: 1.5 × 3 = 4.5. Days: 90 ÷ 4.5 = 20 days.

n.1: 60 days divides 90 by 1.5 tablets and ignores the three doses each day.
n.2: 135 days multiplies 90 by 1.5 instead of dividing.
n.3: 30 days divides 90 by 3 doses and ignores the 1.5 tablets per dose.

M.q: A clinic records each new patient's blood type (A, B, AB, or O) to help plan its blood supply. Which measure of center can be used to describe these data?
o: The median
The weighted mean
The mode
The mean
M.w: Blood type is categorical data with no numeric values or natural order, so the mode (the most common type) is the only usable measure of center.

n.0: A median needs values that can be put in a meaningful order; A, B, AB and O have none.
n.1: A weighted mean also needs numeric values to multiply by the weights.
n.3: A mean needs numeric values to add, and blood types are categories.

M.q: A phlebotomist earns $27.50 per hour plus a flat $165 weekly bonus. Her pay for one week was $1,210, so 27.5h + 165 = 1,210. How many hours, h, did she work that week? Enter the number of hours.

tr.44: Divided 1,210 by 27.50 without first subtracting the $165 bonus.
tr.50: Added the bonus to 1,210 instead of subtracting it.

M.w: Subtract the bonus from both sides: 27.5h = 1,210 - 165 = 1,045. Divide by 27.5: h = 1,045 ÷ 27.5 = 38 hours. Check: 27.5 × 38 = 1,045, and 1,045 + 165 = 1,210.

M.q: A patient-education poster is enlarged proportionally from a draft that is 8 inches wide and 10 inches tall. The poster is 26 inches wide. How tall is the poster? Enter the number of inches.

tr.28: Added the 18-inch increase in width to the height instead of scaling.
tr.20.8: Set up the ratio upside down (26 × 8 ÷ 10).

M.w: Set up width/height: 8/10 = 26/h. Cross-multiply: 8h = 260, so h = 32.5 inches.

M.q: A child weighs 44 pounds. The provider orders one dose of a medication at 10 milligrams per kilogram of body weight. The oral suspension contains 40 milligrams in every 5 milliliters. Use 1 kilogram = 2.2 pounds. How many milliliters make up one dose?
o: 5 mL
55 mL
25 mL
121 mL

n.0: 200 ÷ 40 = 5 is the number of 5 mL portions in the dose; multiply by 5 mL to get 25 mL.
n.1: This uses the weight in pounds without converting to kilograms (44 × 10 = 440 mg; 440 ÷ 40 × 5 = 55 mL).
n.3: This multiplies 44 by 2.2 (96.8 kg) instead of dividing, which gives 968 mg and 121 mL.

M.q: On an easy 20-point quiz, most students scored from 18 to 20 points, and a few students scored between 5 and 10 points. Which describes the shape of the score distribution and how its mean compares with its median?
o: Skewed right; the mean is greater than the median
Skewed left; the mean is greater than the median
Skewed left; the mean is less than the median
Skewed right; the mean is less than the median
M.w: The few low scores form a long tail on the left, so the distribution is skewed left. Those low scores pull the mean down below the median.

n.0: This names the skew by where the scores pile up (the right); skew is named for the tail, which is on the left.
n.1: The shape is right, but the low tail pulls the mean below the median, not above it.
n.3: The tail is on the left, so the distribution is skewed left, not right.

M.q: At the same time of day, a 6-foot-tall nurse casts a shadow 4 feet long, and a flagpole outside the clinic casts a shadow 22 feet long. The two right triangles formed are similar. How tall is the flagpole?
o: 33 ft
24 ft
132 ft
M.w: Height to shadow is the same in both triangles: 6/4 = h/22. h = 22 × 6 ÷ 4 = 33 ft.

n.1: This sets up the ratio upside down (22 × 4 ÷ 6).
n.2: This adds the 2-foot difference between height and shadow; similar triangles scale by multiplying.
n.3: This multiplies 6 by 22 but does not divide by the 4-foot shadow.

M.q: An urgent care clinic bills a $40 visit fee plus $25 for each lab test. A patient's bill came to $165. Which equation can be used to find t, the number of lab tests the patient had?
M.w: Total = fixed fee + rate × quantity, so 25t + 40 = 165. Solving: 25t = 125, so t = 5 lab tests.

n.0: The $40 fee is already part of the $165 bill, so it is subtracted from 165, not added: 25t = 165 - 40.
n.2: This multiplies the visit fee by 25 as well. The $40 is a one-time charge that is added to 25t.
n.3: This swaps the rate and the fixed fee: $25 is charged for each test, and $40 is charged once per visit.

M.q: A solution is warmed at a constant rate. Its temperature is 26°C after 4 minutes and 44°C after 10 minutes. What was the temperature of the solution at 0 minutes?
M.w: Rate = (44 - 26) / (10 - 4) = 18 / 6 = 3°C per minute. Going back 4 minutes from 26°C: 26 - 4(3) = 14°C.

n.0: 26 - 18 = 8 subtracts the whole 6-minute change instead of 4 minutes' worth.
n.2: 3°C is the rate of change per minute, not the starting temperature.
n.3: 26 / 4 = 6.5 assumes direct variation (starting at 0°C), but the solution did not start at 0°C.

M.q: To estimate 6.8 × 4.6, a student rounds both numbers to the nearest whole number and calculates 7 × 5 = 35. How does this estimate compare with the exact product?
o: An exact estimate, because the rounding errors are both less than 0.5
An underestimate, because 4.6 was rounded more than 6.8
An overestimate by 0.6, the total amount the factors were rounded up
An overestimate, because both factors were rounded up
M.w: Both factors were rounded up (6.8 → 7 and 4.6 → 5), so the estimate is too high. Exact: 6.8 × 4.6 = 31.28, so 35 is 3.72 too high.

n.0: The rounding errors are small, but they still change the product (35 vs 31.28).
n.1: Rounding both factors up makes the product larger, so the estimate is too high, not too low.
n.2: The round-offs are multiplied by the other factors, so the error is 35 - 31.28 = 3.72, not 0.6.

M.q: It takes 3 aides 8 hours to restock all of a hospital's supply rooms. Working at the same rate, how long would it take 4 aides to do the same job?
o: 10 hours 40 minutes
2 hours
7 hours
6 hours
M.w: This is an inverse proportion: aides × hours stays constant. 3 × 8 = 24 aide-hours, so 4 aides need 24 ÷ 4 = 6 hours.

n.0: This treats the relationship as direct. More aides finish faster, so the time must decrease.
n.1: This divides the original 8 hours by 4 aides and ignores that the 8 hours was for 3 aides.
n.2: This subtracts 1 hour for the 1 extra aide. The total work, 24 aide-hours, stays the same.

M.q: A study asks whether a person's resting heart rate is affected by the number of cups of coffee the person drinks per day. What is the independent variable in this study?
o: Time of day heart rate is measured
Resting heart rate
Cups of coffee per day
The people in the study
M.w: The study tests the effect of coffee intake on heart rate. Coffee intake is the possible cause (independent); heart rate is the response (dependent).

n.0: Measurement time should be held the same, which makes it a controlled variable.
n.1: Heart rate is named first, but it is the outcome being affected, so it is dependent.
n.3: The participants are the sample, not a variable.

M.q: A histogram shows the systolic blood pressures of 50 adults: 100-109, 6 adults; 110-119, 14 adults; 120-129, 17 adults; 130-139, 9 adults; 140-149, 4 adults. Which statement must be true?
o: Over half the adults had pressures of 130 or above
Exactly 4 adults had a systolic pressure of 140
The median pressure is in the 120-129 interval
The most common single reading was 125
M.w: With 50 values, the median is the mean of the 25th and 26th values. Running totals: 6, then 20, then 37. The 25th and 26th values both fall in the 120-129 interval.

n.0: Only 9 + 4 = 13 of 50 adults (26%) were at 130 or above.
n.1: The 4 adults are somewhere in 140-149; a histogram does not show exact values.
n.3: The tallest bar shows the most common interval, not any single reading.

M.q: A $120 stethoscope is marked 25% off. At checkout, a coupon takes an additional 10% off the sale price. What is the final price of the stethoscope, before tax?
M.w: Successive discounts multiply. After 25% off: 120 × 0.75 = $90. After another 10% off: 90 × 0.90 = $81. The total discount is 32.5%, not 35%.

n.1: This applies the 10% coupon but not the 25% markdown.
n.2: This adds the discounts to get 35% off. The 10% applies to the $90 sale price, not to $120.
n.3: This applies the 25% markdown but not the 10% coupon.

M.q: A wooden deck is shaped like a trapezoid. Its parallel sides are 18 feet and 12 feet long, and the perpendicular distance between them is 8 feet. What is the area of the deck?
o: 120 ft²
144 ft²
240 ft²
96 ft²

n.1: This multiplies the longer base by the height, as if the deck were a rectangle.
n.2: This adds the bases and multiplies by the height but leaves out the 1/2.
n.3: This multiplies the shorter base by the height, as if the deck were a rectangle.

M.q: Maya's monthly budget of $2,400 is shown in a pie chart: Rent 35%, Food 15%, Transportation 12.5%, Savings 10%, Other 27.5%. How much more does she budget for rent than for food and transportation combined?
M.w: Amount = percent x total. Rent: 0.35 x 2,400 = $840. Food: 0.15 x 2,400 = $360. Transportation: 0.125 x 2,400 = $300. Food + transportation = $660. Difference: 840 - 660 = $180.

n.1: 840 - 300 = $540 compares rent with transportation only.
n.2: 840 - 360 = $480 compares rent with food only.
n.3: $660 is the food and transportation total, not how much more rent is.

M.q: A bottle holds 250 mL of a liquid medication. The prescribed dose is 7.5 mL twice a day. How many full days will the bottle last?
o: 17 days
33 days
34 days
16 days
M.w: Daily use: 7.5 × 2 = 15 mL. Days: 250 ÷ 15 = 16.67. Only complete days count, so round down to 16 days (16 × 15 = 240 mL).

n.0: This rounds 16.67 up. After 16 days only 10 mL is left, which is not enough for both doses on day 17.
n.1: This is the number of full doses (250 ÷ 7.5), not days; there are 2 doses per day.
n.2: This rounds the number of doses (33.3) up and treats each dose as a day.

M.q: A student writes each pair of variables in the form (independent variable, dependent variable). Which pair is written in the correct order?
o: (Hours worked at $18 per hour, weekly paycheck)
(Weekly grocery bill, number of people in the household)
(Distance traveled, hours driven at a steady speed)
(Crop yield, inches of rainfall)
M.w: The paycheck is calculated from the hours worked, so hours worked is independent and the paycheck is dependent; the pair is in the correct order.

n.1: The grocery bill depends on household size, so the order is reversed.
n.2: At a steady speed, distance depends on the hours driven, so the order is reversed.
n.3: Crop yield depends on rainfall, so the order is reversed.

M.q: A prescriber orders 0.15 mg of a drug for each kilogram of body weight. The patient weighs 72.6 kg. What is the dose? Do not round until the final answer, and round it to the nearest tenth of a milligram. Enter the number only.

tr.11: Rounded the weight to 73 kg first (0.15 × 73 = 10.95, which rounds to 11.0).

M.w: Dose = 0.15 × 72.6 = 10.89 mg. Round only at the end: the hundredths digit is 9, so 10.89 → 10.9 mg.

M.q: Jordan finishes a 10-kilometer charity run in 50 minutes. Use 1 mile = 1.6 kilometers. What was Jordan's average speed for the run in miles per hour?
o: 12 mph
7.5 mph
19.2 mph
12.5 mph

n.0: 12 is the speed in kilometers per hour; convert 10 km to 6.25 mi first.
n.2: This multiplies 10 km by 1.6; kilometers to miles means dividing by 1.6.
n.3: This treats 50 minutes as 0.5 hour; 50 min = 50/60 of an hour.

M.q: A uniform store records the sizes of the last 10 pairs of nursing clogs it sold: 8, 9, 7.5, 9, 10, 8, 9, 11, 8.5, 9. What is the mode of the sizes sold?
M.w: The mode is the value that occurs most often. Size 9 appears 4 times, more than any other size.

n.0: 89 / 10 = 8.9 is the mean of the sizes.
n.1: Size 8 appears only twice, fewer times than size 9.
n.3: 4 is how many times size 9 appears, not the size itself.

M.q: A rectangular fish tank in a pediatric waiting room measures 50 centimeters long, 30 centimeters wide, and 40 centimeters high. How many liters of water does the tank hold when it is completely full?
o: 6 L

n.0: This divides 60,000 cm³ by 100; 1 L = 1,000 cm³.
n.2: This divides 60,000 cm³ by 10,000 instead of 1,000.
n.3: 60,000 is the volume in cubic centimeters (milliliters), not liters.

M.q: The diameter of a human red blood cell is about 0.0000075 meter. How is this length written in scientific notation?
M.w: Move the decimal point right until one nonzero digit is in front of it: 0.0000075 → 7.5 takes 6 moves. Moving right for a small number gives a negative exponent: 7.5 × 10⁻⁶.

n.0: 7.5 × 10⁻⁷ = 0.00000075, which has one zero too many; reaching 7.5 from 0.0000075 takes 6 moves, not 7.
n.1: A positive exponent gives a large number (7,500,000); a number less than 1 needs a negative exponent.
n.2: This counts only 5 moves; 7.5 × 10⁻⁵ = 0.000075.

M.q: A patient is prescribed 1 tablespoon of cough syrup three times a day for 5 days. The pharmacy needs the total volume in milliliters. How many milliliters of cough syrup will the patient take over the full 5 days?
o: 150 mL
225 mL
45 mL
75 mL
M.w: 1 tbsp = 15 mL. Per day: 3 × 15 = 45 mL. For 5 days: 45 × 5 = 225 mL.

n.0: This uses 10 mL per tablespoon (2 teaspoons); 1 tbsp = 3 tsp = 15 mL.
n.2: This is one day's amount (3 × 15 mL); the course lasts 5 days.
n.3: This uses 5 mL, the volume of a teaspoon; 1 tbsp = 15 mL.

S.q: A 54-gram metal sample is lowered into a graduated cylinder, and the water level rises from 30.0 mL to 50.0 mL. What is the density of the metal in grams per milliliter? Enter your answer rounded to the nearest tenth.

tr.1.8: Divided by the starting water level (30 mL) instead of the volume displaced.
tr.1.1: Divided by the final water level (50 mL) instead of the volume displaced.
tr.0.4: Divided volume by mass (20 / 54) instead of mass by volume.

S.w: Step 1: volume by water displacement = 50.0 mL - 30.0 mL = 20.0 mL. Step 2: density = mass / volume = 54 g / 20.0 mL = 2.7 g/mL.

S.q: The lining of the urinary bladder must stretch as the bladder fills and then return to its resting shape as it empties. Which tissue lines the bladder?
o: Transitional epithelium
Stratified squamous epithelium
Simple columnar epithelium
