Dense regular connective tissue
S.w: Transitional epithelium is a stretchable epithelium whose cells change shape as the organ fills and empties. It lines the urinary bladder.

n.1: Stratified squamous epithelium is layered and protective (as in the epidermis) but is not the stretchable bladder lining.
n.2: Simple columnar epithelium is a single layer of tall cells, as in the lining of the GI tract; it does not stretch like the bladder lining.
n.3: Dense regular connective tissue forms tendons and ligaments; it is not a lining tissue.

S.q: A 56-year-old woman has gone through menopause, and her ovaries no longer contain functioning follicles. Which pattern of hormone levels is expected in her blood?
o: High estrogen and progesterone with low FSH and LH
Low estrogen and progesterone with low FSH and LH
Low estrogen and progesterone with high FSH and LH
Low estrogen with high progesterone and low FSH
S.w: Two steps. (1) With the follicles exhausted, the ovaries make little estrogen and progesterone. (2) Those hormones normally exert negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, so without them FSH and LH rise.

n.0: Without functioning follicles the ovaries cannot keep estrogen and progesterone high.
n.1: Falling ovarian hormones remove negative feedback, so FSH and LH rise rather than fall.
n.3: Progesterone comes mainly from the corpus luteum, which forms after ovulation, so it is low after menopause; FSH is high.

S.q: A culture starts with one bacterial cell. It divides by binary fission every 20 minutes, and every new cell keeps dividing at that rate. Enter the number of cells after 2 hours as a whole number.

tr.7: Counted 1 cell plus 1 new cell per generation (1 + 6).
tr.12: Added 2 cells per generation (6 x 2), a linear doubling instead of exponential growth.

S.w: Step 1: 2 hours = 120 minutes, and 120 / 20 = 6 generations. Step 2: each generation doubles the population (exponential growth), so the count after n generations is 2^n = 2^6 = 64 cells (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64).

S.q: Research journals require scientists to describe their methods in enough detail for other researchers to follow. What is the main scientific purpose of this requirement?
o: It lets readers apply the results to any population.
It lets editors judge the authors' expertise and reputation.
It lets reviewers confirm that the hypothesis has been proven.
It lets other scientists repeat the work and check the results.
S.w: Scientific explanations must be reproducible. Detailed methods let independent scientists replicate the study, and peer review and replication check whether the conclusions hold.

n.0: Detailed methods show exactly who and what was studied, which limits the conclusions to that population rather than extending them.
n.1: Judging a claim by the authors' authority is not evidence; methods are described so the work itself can be checked.
n.2: Evidence supports a hypothesis but never proves it; methods are shared so the work can be checked, and possibly refuted.

S.q: Place the vessels in the order that blood flows through them as it passes through a kidney, starting with the first.
o: Renal vein
Glomerulus
Afferent arteriole
Renal artery
Peritubular capillaries
Efferent arteriole
S.w: Blood arrives in the renal artery and its branches, enters each glomerulus through an afferent arteriole, leaves through an efferent arteriole into the peritubular capillaries around the tubule, and finally drains into the renal vein.

S.q: Carbon dioxide produced by working muscle must be carried to the lungs. In which form is most of this carbon dioxide transported in the blood?
o: Bound to hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin
Bound to the iron atoms of heme groups
Dissolved as carbon dioxide gas in plasma
As bicarbonate ions in the plasma
S.w: About 70% of CO₂ is carried as bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻), formed inside red blood cells by carbonic anhydrase and then moved into the plasma. About 20-23% rides on hemoglobin and 7-10% is dissolved.

n.0: Carbaminohemoglobin carries only about a fifth of the CO₂, not most of it.
n.1: Iron in heme binds oxygen; CO₂ that binds hemoglobin attaches to the globin protein, and it is still the minority route.
n.2: Only about 7-10% of CO₂ is carried dissolved in plasma.

S.q: Which of the following disorders results from the immune system attacking the body's own tissues?
o: Osteoarthritis of the knees
Hay fever triggered by pollen
Type 2 diabetes mellitus
Rheumatoid arthritis
S.w: In autoimmune disease the immune system attacks self antigens. In rheumatoid arthritis it attacks the synovial membranes of the joints. Other examples include type 1 diabetes, lupus, multiple sclerosis, Hashimoto's thyroiditis and Graves' disease.

n.0: Osteoarthritis is wear-and-tear breakdown of articular cartilage, not an immune attack; rheumatoid arthritis is the autoimmune joint disease.
n.1: Hay fever is an IgE-mediated allergy (hypersensitivity) to a foreign antigen, pollen, not an attack on self tissue.
n.2: Type 2 diabetes is caused by insulin resistance; it is type 1 diabetes in which the immune system destroys the pancreatic beta cells.

S.q: Over several years, a pharmacist notices that each patient she sees taking a certain allergy drug reports drowsiness. She concludes that the drug causes drowsiness in people who take it. Which describes her reasoning?
o: Inductive, moving from specific cases to a general conclusion
Inductive, moving from a general rule to a specific case
Deductive, moving from specific cases to a general conclusion
Deductive, moving from a general rule to a specific case
S.w: Inductive reasoning builds a general conclusion from specific observations. Its conclusions are probable, not certain: one patient who does not become drowsy could overturn the generalization.

n.1: This pairs inductive with the deductive direction; she reasoned from cases to a rule.
n.2: Specific-to-general is inductive; this pairs the right direction with the wrong name.
n.3: Deductive reasoning does go from a general rule to a specific case, but she started from individual patients.

S.q: During a lumbar puncture, a needle is inserted between two lumbar vertebrae into the fluid-filled space of the vertebral canal. Which body cavity, and its larger division, does this space belong to?
o: The cranial cavity, part of the ventral cavity
The mediastinum, part of the thoracic cavity
The pelvic cavity, part of the ventral cavity
The vertebral cavity, part of the dorsal cavity
S.w: The spinal cord lies in the vertebral (spinal) cavity. Together with the cranial cavity, it forms the dorsal body cavity, protected by bone and meninges.

n.0: The cranial cavity holds the brain, and it belongs to the dorsal cavity, not the ventral cavity.
n.1: The mediastinum is in the ventral thoracic cavity and holds the heart, trachea and esophagus, not the spinal cord.
n.2: The pelvic cavity holds the bladder, rectum and reproductive organs; the spinal cord lies in the dorsal cavity.

S.q: A chemist adds a catalyst to a reaction mixture that has already reached equilibrium. What happens to the equilibrium amounts of reactants and products?
o: They stay the same, because both rates rise equally
They shift toward more products, as the forward rate rises
They shift toward more reactants, as the reverse rate rises
They change as the catalyst is gradually used up
S.w: A catalyst lowers the activation energy for the forward and reverse reactions equally, so both rates increase by the same factor. Equilibrium is reached faster, but the equilibrium amounts do not change, and the catalyst is not consumed.

n.1: The forward rate does rise, but the reverse rate rises equally, so there is no net shift toward products.
n.2: The reverse rate rises, but by the same factor as the forward rate, so there is no shift toward reactants.
n.3: A catalyst is not consumed by the reaction; it is recovered unchanged at the end.

S.q: Place the steps for balancing a chemical equation in the order a student should perform them, starting with the first.
o: Recount the atoms to confirm every element is balanced
Count the atoms of each element on both sides of the arrow
Write the correct formulas for all reactants and products
Add coefficients to balance one element at a time
S.w: First write correct formulas, which are never changed afterward. Then count the atoms of each element on each side, adjust coefficients one element at a time, and finally recount to check that every element balances (using the smallest whole-number coefficients).

S.q: During anaphase I of meiosis in a human testis, which structures separate and move to opposite poles of the cell?
o: Single chromatids drawn from all four strands of each tetrad
Haploid daughter cells pinched apart at a cleavage furrow
Homologous chromosomes, each still made of two chromatids
Sister chromatids, each becoming its own chromosome
S.w: Anaphase I separates homologous chromosomes; each still consists of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere. Sister chromatids separate later, in anaphase II.

n.0: The four chromatids of a tetrad do not split up individually in anaphase I; whole homologs, each with two chromatids, move apart.
n.1: Pinching apart the cytoplasm is cytokinesis, which follows telophase; it is not what moves to the poles in anaphase I.
n.3: Sister chromatids separate in anaphase II of meiosis and in mitotic anaphase, not in anaphase I.

S.q: Neon is used in lighted signs partly because it does not react with the glass tube or the metal electrodes. What best explains neon's very low chemical reactivity?
o: Its outer shell is already full with 8 electrons
Its 8 valence electrons are easily shared in bonds
Its single valence electron is held very tightly
Its large atomic radius keeps other atoms away
S.w: Neon is a noble gas (group 18). Its outer shell is full (2, 8), so it has no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons, which makes it very unreactive.

n.1: A full octet is stable; neon does not share its valence electrons to form bonds.
n.2: Neon has 8 valence electrons, not 1. A single valence electron describes the very reactive alkali metals.
n.3: Size does not explain it: argon and krypton are larger noble gases and are also unreactive, because they too have a full outer shell.

S.q: For a gene with complete dominance, A is dominant over a. Which crosses can produce offspring showing the recessive phenotype? Select all that apply.
o: aa x aa
AA x AA
AA x aa
Aa x aa
AA x Aa
Aa x Aa
S.w: A recessive phenotype needs aa, so each parent must be able to pass on a. Aa x Aa (1/4 aa), Aa x aa (1/2 aa) and aa x aa (all aa) can all produce it.

n.1: AA x AA gives only AA offspring.
n.2: AA x aa gives only Aa offspring, all showing the dominant phenotype.
n.4: AA x Aa gives AA and Aa offspring; the AA parent always passes on A.

S.q: A surgeon reattaches a torn tendon to the outer surface of a long bone. Which structure covers that surface, carries blood vessels and nerves, and adds bone to increase the bone's width?
o: Articular cartilage
Endosteum
Periosteum
Synovial membrane
S.w: The periosteum is the outer membrane of a bone: it carries vessels and nerves, anchors tendons, and adds bone to the surface (appositional growth in width) and during repair.

n.0: Articular cartilage covers joint surfaces, is avascular and does not anchor tendons or add width.
n.1: The endosteum lines the internal medullary cavity, not the outer surface where tendons attach.
n.3: The synovial membrane lines a joint capsule and secretes synovial fluid; tendons do not anchor to it.

S.q: A nurse asks a patient to raise the arm out to the side until it is level with the shoulder. Which muscle is the prime mover for this abduction of the arm?
o: Pectoralis major
Latissimus dorsi
Trapezius
Deltoid
S.w: The deltoid, which caps the shoulder, is the prime mover of arm abduction (moving the arm away from the midline). It is also a common intramuscular injection site.

n.0: The pectoralis major flexes, adducts and medially rotates the arm.
n.1: The latissimus dorsi extends and adducts the arm, the opposite direction to abduction.
n.2: The trapezius elevates and retracts the scapula and extends the head; it does not abduct the arm at the shoulder joint.

S.q: Vital capacity is the largest volume of air a person can exhale after taking the deepest possible breath. Which volumes add up to vital capacity?
o: Tidal volume + inspiratory reserve volume + residual volume
Inspiratory reserve volume + expiratory reserve volume + residual volume
Tidal volume + inspiratory reserve volume + expiratory reserve volume
Tidal volume + expiratory reserve volume + residual volume
S.w: Vital capacity = tidal volume + inspiratory reserve volume + expiratory reserve volume: everything that can be moved in and out. Residual volume stays in the lungs and is excluded.

n.0: Residual volume cannot be exhaled, so it is not part of vital capacity; expiratory reserve volume is missing.
n.1: This leaves out tidal volume and wrongly includes residual volume.
n.3: This leaves out inspiratory reserve volume and wrongly includes residual volume.

S.q: Which statements about the conduction system of the heart are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: The AV node normally fires faster than the SA node
Purkinje fibers spread the impulse through the ventricular walls
The bundle branches run down the interventricular septum
The SA node lies in the wall of the right atrium
The bundle of His carries impulses from the ventricles up to the atria
S.w: The SA node (right atrial wall) starts the impulse; the AV node delays it; the bundle of His and the right and left bundle branches carry it down the interventricular septum; Purkinje fibers spread it through the ventricles so they contract from the apex upward.

n.0: The AV node's intrinsic rate (about 40 to 60 per minute) is slower than the SA node's, which is why the SA node leads.
n.4: The bundle of His carries impulses downward from the AV node toward the ventricles, not back up to the atria.

S.q: Which sweat glands are distributed over most of the body surface, open directly onto the skin through pores, and secrete watery sweat that cools the body?
o: Sebaceous glands
Eccrine glands
Ceruminous glands
Apocrine glands
S.w: Eccrine (merocrine) sweat glands are the most numerous, are found almost everywhere (especially palms, soles and forehead), open onto the surface through pores and secrete watery sweat for thermoregulation.

n.0: Sebaceous glands secrete oily sebum, usually into hair follicles; they do not produce sweat.
n.2: Ceruminous glands are modified sweat glands in the ear canal that produce earwax.
n.3: Apocrine glands are found in the axillary and anogenital regions, open into hair follicles and become active at puberty.

S.q: An antacid containing magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)₂, is taken to neutralize excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach. What are the products of this neutralization reaction?
o: Magnesium chloride and hydrogen gas
Magnesium chloride and carbon dioxide
Magnesium chloride and water
Magnesium oxide and chlorine gas
S.w: Acid + base → salt + water. Mg(OH)₂ + 2 HCl → MgCl₂ + 2 H₂O: the salt is magnesium chloride, and H⁺ from the acid joins OH⁻ from the base to form water.

n.0: Hydrogen gas forms when an acid reacts with an active metal, not with a hydroxide base.
n.1: Carbon dioxide forms when an acid reacts with a carbonate antacid (such as CaCO₃); magnesium hydroxide contains no carbon.
n.3: Neutralization swaps ions to give a salt and water; it does not produce chlorine gas or an oxide.

S.q: Which statement correctly describes the cell that the ovary releases at ovulation and the stage its meiosis has reached?
o: A mature ovum that completed meiosis II before leaving the ovary
A secondary oocyte that completes meiosis II if it is fertilized
A primary oocyte that completes meiosis I in the uterine tube
A secondary oocyte that completed meiosis II at the LH surge
S.w: Primary oocytes stay arrested in prophase I from before birth until puberty. Each cycle, one completes meiosis I just before ovulation, forming a secondary oocyte and the first polar body. The secondary oocyte is released and finishes meiosis II only if a sperm fertilizes it.

n.0: Meiosis II is not finished before ovulation; it is completed after fertilization.
n.2: Meiosis I is completed just before ovulation, so the released cell is already a secondary oocyte.
n.3: The LH surge is followed by completion of meiosis I, not meiosis II; meiosis II waits for fertilization.

S.q: Parietal cells in the stomach lining secrete hydrochloric acid, which keeps gastric pH very low. Which of the following is a role of this acid?
o: Binding vitamin B12 for uptake in the ileum
Emulsifying fat droplets so lipase can act
Activating pancreatic trypsinogen into trypsin
Converting pepsinogen into active pepsin
S.w: Hydrochloric acid activates pepsinogen into pepsin, which begins protein digestion, and it kills many swallowed microbes.

n.0: Binding vitamin B12 is the role of intrinsic factor, the other product of parietal cells, not the acid.
n.1: Emulsifying fat is the job of bile salts in the duodenum, not stomach acid.
n.2: Trypsinogen is activated in the duodenum by the brush-border enzyme enteropeptidase (and then by trypsin itself), not by stomach acid.

S.q: Normal saline used for IV fluids is 0.9% (w/v) sodium chloride. How many grams of sodium chloride are dissolved in 1 liter of normal saline?
o: 9 g
S.w: Step 1: % (w/v) means grams of solute per 100 mL of solution, so 0.9% is 0.9 g per 100 mL. Step 2: 1 liter is 1,000 mL, or 10 x 100 mL, so the bag holds 0.9 x 10 = 9 g of NaCl.

n.0: 0.9 g is the amount in 100 mL, not in a full liter.
n.1: 0.09 g misplaces the decimal point; it is ten times too small even for 100 mL, let alone a liter.
n.3: 90 g would be a 9% solution; this moves the decimal point one place too far.

S.q: In winter, a layer of ice forms on top of a pond while liquid water remains below it. Which statement correctly explains why ice floats on liquid water?
o: Molecules in ice move faster than in liquid, so they spread farther apart
Ice has fewer hydrogen bonds than water, so it is less dense
Trapped air in the crystals lowers the density of ice below that of water
Hydrogen bonds lock ice into an open lattice that is less dense than water
S.w: When water freezes, hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open, hexagonal lattice that takes up more space than the liquid. Ice is therefore less dense than liquid water and floats; water is densest at about 4 °C.

n.0: Molecules in a solid move less, not more, than in the liquid; they vibrate in fixed positions.
n.1: Ice has more hydrogen bonds, not fewer: each molecule is locked to four neighbors, and that rigid open network is what lowers its density.
n.2: Pure, clear ice with no bubbles still floats. The low density comes from the hydrogen-bonded lattice, not trapped air.

S.q: A biology class is planning an investigation on pea plants and light. Which statement is written as a testable scientific hypothesis?
o: Pea plants should be given as many hours of light as a grower can provide.
Pea plants grown under bright light are more attractive than shaded ones.
Do pea plants grow taller when they receive more hours of light each day?
If pea plants get 8 hours of light daily instead of 4, they will grow taller.
S.w: A hypothesis is a testable, tentative prediction, often in "If ... then ..." form. Plant height can be measured under two light conditions, so this statement can be supported or refuted by data.

n.0: This is a recommendation about what growers should do, not a prediction that can be tested.
n.1: "More attractive" is an opinion that cannot be measured objectively, so it is not testable.
n.2: This is the research question; a hypothesis is a statement that predicts an answer.

S.q: A drug molecule shaped like an enzyme's substrate binds to the active site and slows the reaction. Adding much more substrate restores the normal rate. Which type of inhibition is this?
o: Noncompetitive inhibition
Competitive inhibition
Substrate saturation
Denaturation by heat
S.w: A competitive inhibitor binds the active site and competes with the substrate, so raising substrate concentration can overcome it.

n.0: A noncompetitive (allosteric) inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the enzyme's shape; extra substrate does not overcome it.
n.2: Saturation is the plateau reached when all active sites are busy; it is not inhibition.
n.3: Denaturation is loss of enzyme shape from heat or extreme pH, not binding of an inhibitor.

S.q: Hydrogen peroxide stored in a clear bottle slowly breaks down when exposed to light, according to the equation 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂. Which type of reaction is this?
o: Decomposition
Single replacement
Combustion
Synthesis
S.w: A decomposition reaction (AB → A + B) breaks one compound into two or more simpler substances. Hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen.

n.1: Single replacement needs a free element replacing another in a compound; there is only one reactant here.
n.2: Combustion is a fuel reacting with O₂ to produce CO₂ and H₂O; here O₂ is produced, not consumed.
n.3: Synthesis is the reverse pattern: two or more reactants combine into one product.

S.q: Place the levels of protein structure in order, starting with the simplest level and ending with the most complex.
o: R-group interactions fold the chain into its overall 3-D shape.
Hydrogen bonds along the backbone form helices and pleated sheets.
Amino acids are linked in a specific sequence by peptide bonds.
Two or more folded polypeptide chains join, as in hemoglobin.
S.w: Primary (amino acid sequence) -> secondary (alpha helix and beta pleated sheet from backbone hydrogen bonds) -> tertiary (overall 3-D shape from R-group interactions) -> quaternary (two or more chains, such as the four chains of hemoglobin).

S.q: A graduated cylinder holds 42.0 mL of water. A student lowers a small stone into it, and the level rises to 57.5 mL. A balance shows the stone's mass is 31.0 g. What is the density of the stone?
o: 2.0 g/mL
S.w: Step 1: volume by water displacement = final level - initial level = 57.5 mL - 42.0 mL = 15.5 mL. Step 2: density = mass / volume = 31.0 g / 15.5 mL = 2.0 g/mL.

n.0: This divides volume by mass (15.5 / 31.0); density is mass divided by volume.
n.1: This divides the mass by the final water level (31.0 / 57.5) instead of by the displaced volume.
n.2: This divides the mass by the starting water level (31.0 / 42.0) instead of by the change in level.

S.q: A bathroom scale shows 62.0 kg each of five times a person steps on it. A calibrated clinic scale shows the person's true mass is 60.0 kg. How is the bathroom scale best described?
o: Valid but not reliable
Reliable but not valid
Both reliable and valid
Neither reliable nor valid
S.w: Reliability is consistency: the scale gives the same reading every time. Validity is measuring what it claims to measure: it is consistently 2 kg off the true mass, so it is not valid.

n.0: This swaps the terms: identical repeated readings mean the scale is reliable.
n.2: A consistent 2 kg error means the readings do not reflect the true mass, so the scale is not valid.
n.3: The five identical readings show the scale is reliable.

S.q: Two sisters with the same parents differ genetically partly because segments were exchanged between homologous chromosomes while their parents' gametes formed. When does this exchange take place?
o: Metaphase of mitosis
Prophase II of meiosis
Anaphase I of meiosis
Prophase I of meiosis
S.w: Crossing over happens in prophase I, when homologous chromosomes pair up (synapsis) as tetrads and exchange segments.

n.0: Homologous chromosomes do not pair in mitosis, so there is no crossing over.
n.1: Homologs are no longer paired in prophase II, so crossing over between them does not occur then.
n.2: Anaphase I is when homologs separate; the exchange had already happened in prophase I.

S.q: In a leaf cell, water molecules are split and oxygen gas is released during photosynthesis. Where in the chloroplast does this happen?
o: In the inner membrane, during electron transport
In the thylakoids, during the light reactions
In the cytoplasm, during glycolysis
In the stroma, during the Calvin cycle
S.w: The light-dependent reactions take place in the thylakoid membranes. There water is split, O₂ is released, and ATP and NADPH are made for the Calvin cycle.

n.0: Electron transport on an inner membrane that ends with O₂ forming water describes mitochondria, the reverse of releasing O₂.
n.2: Glycolysis in the cytoplasm is part of respiration and neither splits water nor releases oxygen.
n.3: The Calvin cycle in the stroma fixes CO₂ into sugar; it does not split water.

S.q: A student sorting metric rulers and measuring tools by scale is asked to rank five lengths. Place the lengths in order from largest to smallest, starting with the largest.
o: 1 micrometer
1 centimeter
1 dekameter
1 kilometer
1 decimeter
S.w: 1 km = 1,000 m; 1 dam = 10 m; 1 dm = 0.1 m; 1 cm = 0.01 m; 1 micrometer = 0.000001 m (10⁻⁶ m). Deka (10) and deci (0.1) sound alike but sit on opposite sides of the base unit: King Henry Died By Drinking Chocolate Milk (kilo, hecto, deka, base, deci, centi, milli), with micro three steps below milli.

S.q: A class measures an enzyme's activity at three temperatures. Data: 20 °C, 12 units; 30 °C, 24 units; 40 °C, 36 units. Which estimate of the activity at 35 °C is best supported by the data?
o: About 36 units
About 48 units
About 30 units
About 24 units
S.w: Activity rises 12 units for every 10 °C across the tested range, so halfway between 30 °C and 40 °C it should be about halfway between 24 and 36: about 30 units. Estimating between measured points (interpolation) is reliable.

n.0: 36 units is the measured value at 40 °C; 35 °C is only halfway there.
n.1: 48 units would follow the trend to 50 °C, beyond the range tested, not 35 °C.
n.3: 24 units is the measured value at 30 °C; the trend predicts a higher value at 35 °C.

S.q: A student is preparing a summary of what separates a scientific explanation from other kinds of claims. Which features make an explanation scientific? Select all that apply.
o: It is accepted because experts hold it.
It can be reproduced by other scientists.
It is testable and could be falsified.
It rests on many personal stories.
It is based on empirical evidence.
It is proven and closed to revision.
S.w: Scientific explanations rest on empirical evidence (observation and measurement), are testable and falsifiable, and are reproducible by others. They stay open to revision when new evidence appears.

n.0: Authority is not evidence; experts' claims must still be backed by data.
n.3: Personal stories are anecdotal evidence, which lacks controls and cannot establish cause.
n.5: Scientific explanations stay open to revision; evidence supports them but does not prove them.

S.q: A hospital places a patient with active tuberculosis in a negative-pressure room and staff wear fitted respirators. Which feature of tuberculosis transmission explains these precautions?
o: TB spreads mainly on objects such as bed rails and doorknobs.
TB bacteria travel in tiny particles that stay suspended in air.
TB is caused by a virus that passes through surgical masks.
TB spreads mainly in large droplets that fall within 2 meters.
S.w: Tuberculosis (bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis) is spread by the airborne route: tiny particles stay suspended and travel on air currents, so airflow control and respirators are needed.

n.0: Spread by contaminated objects (fomites) would call for surface cleaning, not special airflow; TB spreads through the air.
n.2: Tuberculosis is caused by a bacterium, not a virus.
n.3: Large droplets that fall within about 1 to 2 meters describe droplet spread, as with influenza; TB is airborne.

S.q: During elbow flexion, the biceps brachii pulls the radius toward the shoulder while its attachments on the scapula stay fixed. How is the attachment on the radius classified?
o: Origin, because it is on the bone that moves
Origin, because it is farther from the trunk
Insertion, because it is on the bone that moves
Insertion, because it is on the stationary bone
S.w: The origin is the attachment on the more stationary bone (here the scapula); the insertion is on the bone that moves (the radius). During contraction the insertion is pulled toward the origin.

n.0: The attachment on the moving bone is the insertion; the origin is on the more stationary bone.
n.1: Origin and insertion are defined by which bone moves, not by distance from the trunk; the moving radius carries the insertion.
n.3: The insertion is on the bone that moves; the stationary attachment is the origin.

S.q: A student checks a worksheet in which every value should be written in correct scientific notation. Which values are written correctly? Select all that apply.
S.w: Scientific notation is a × 10ⁿ with 1 <= a < 10. The coefficients 4.07, 1.0 and 9.99 all fall in that range; a negative exponent is allowed.

n.0: The coefficient 12.5 is 10 or greater; written correctly it is 1.25 × 10⁵.
n.1: A coefficient of 10 is not less than 10; written correctly it is 1 × 10³.
n.4: The coefficient 0.75 is less than 1; written correctly it is 7.5 × 10⁻⁴.

S.q: A 64-year-old woman is diagnosed with osteoporosis several years after menopause. Which change in bone remodeling best accounts for her loss of bone mass?
o: Osteoblast formation outpaces osteoclast resorption
Osteoclast resorption outpaces osteoblast formation
Calcitonin rises and stimulates osteoclast resorption
Osteoblasts resorb more matrix as estrogen declines
S.w: Bone is constantly remodeled by osteoblasts (which build) and osteoclasts (which resorb). After menopause estrogen falls, resorption exceeds formation, and bone mass is lost: osteoporosis.

n.0: If formation outpaced resorption, bone mass would increase rather than decrease.
n.2: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts; it does not stimulate bone resorption.
n.3: Osteoblasts build bone; resorbing matrix is the job of osteoclasts.

S.q: Place the structures in the order food passes through them after it is swallowed, starting with the first.
o: Ileum
Esophagus
Duodenum
Stomach
Jejunum
Pharynx
S.w: After the mouth, food passes through the pharynx and down the esophagus to the stomach. Chyme then enters the small intestine in the order duodenum, jejunum, ileum before reaching the cecum.

S.q: A liver cell begins making albumin by copying the albumin gene into messenger RNA. Where does this step take place, and which enzyme carries it out?
o: In the nucleus, by DNA polymerase
In the cytoplasm, by helicase
At the ribosome, by RNA polymerase
In the nucleus, by RNA polymerase
S.w: Copying DNA into mRNA is transcription. In eukaryotes it happens in the nucleus, where RNA polymerase reads the DNA template strand and builds complementary mRNA.

n.0: DNA polymerase copies DNA into DNA during replication, not DNA into RNA.
n.1: Helicase unwinds DNA during replication; transcription happens in the nucleus, not the cytoplasm.
n.2: The ribosome is the site of translation, not transcription.

S.q: A radioactive tracer used for a hospital scan has a half-life of 6 hours. A 40-mg dose is prepared at 8:00 a.m. About how much of the tracer remains undecayed at 2:00 a.m. the next day?
o: 10 mg
5 mg
2.5 mg
S.w: From 8:00 a.m. to 2:00 a.m. is 18 hours, which is 18 / 6 = 3 half-lives. Each half-life halves the amount: 40 mg to 20 mg to 10 mg to 5 mg (1/8 of the original).

n.0: This divides 40 by 3 half-lives. Each half-life halves the amount; it does not remove an equal share.
n.1: 10 mg remains after 2 half-lives (12 hours, at 8:00 p.m.), not after the full 18 hours.
n.3: 2.5 mg would remain after 4 half-lives (24 hours), one half-life too many.

S.q: Which hormone is produced by the anterior pituitary gland and stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete cortisol?
o: GHRH
CRH
TSH
ACTH
S.w: Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) from the anterior pituitary stimulates the adrenal cortex to release cortisol.

n.0: GHRH is a hypothalamic releasing hormone that acts on the anterior pituitary to promote growth hormone release, not on the adrenal cortex.
n.1: CRH is a releasing hormone made by the hypothalamus; it acts on the anterior pituitary, not directly on the adrenal cortex.
n.2: TSH from the anterior pituitary stimulates the thyroid, not the adrenal cortex.

S.q: During protein synthesis, one type of RNA carries a specific amino acid and has a three-base anticodon. Which type of RNA is this?
o: Messenger RNA
Transfer RNA
Ribosomal RNA
Primer RNA
S.w: Transfer RNA (tRNA) carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon that pairs with the matching mRNA codon at the ribosome.

n.0: mRNA carries the codons copied from DNA. It does not carry amino acids, and the anticodon is on tRNA.
n.2: rRNA is the structural and catalytic part of ribosomes; it does not carry amino acids or anticodons.
n.3: Primer RNA is the short strand primase lays down to start DNA replication; it carries no amino acid.

S.q: After a long course of a broad-spectrum antibiotic, a patient develops severe diarrhea caused by an overgrowth of Clostridioides difficile in the colon. Which explanation is most likely?
o: The antibiotic converted harmless gut bacteria into C. difficile.
The antibiotic killed normal gut bacteria that kept C. difficile in check.
The antibiotic caused the patient's own colon cells to divide rapidly.
The antibiotic weakened the colon wall, letting viruses enter.
S.w: Normal microbiota compete with pathogens. Killing them with an antibiotic lets an opportunistic pathogen such as C. difficile overgrow.

n.0: Antibiotics kill or inhibit bacteria; they do not turn one bacterial species into another.
n.2: The diarrhea is caused by an overgrowing pathogen, not by the patient's own cells dividing.
n.3: C. difficile is a bacterium, and the disease here is bacterial overgrowth, not viral entry.

S.q: Place the events of a single action potential in the order they occur, starting with the first.
o: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ rushes in
K⁺ flows out of the cell and the membrane repolarizes
A brief hyperpolarization occurs during the refractory period
Na⁺ channels close and voltage-gated K⁺ channels open
The membrane depolarizes to threshold, about -55 mV
S.w: A stimulus brings the membrane to threshold (about -55 mV). Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels then open and Na⁺ rushes in (depolarization). Next the Na⁺ channels close and K⁺ channels open, so K⁺ flows out and the membrane repolarizes. A brief hyperpolarization follows during the refractory period.

S.q: Which photoreceptors are concentrated in the fovea centralis of the retina and provide color vision and sharp detail in bright light?
o: Cones
Hair cells
Rods
Bipolar neurons
S.w: Cones detect color and fine detail in bright light and are concentrated in the fovea centralis.

n.1: Hair cells are the sensory receptors of the cochlea and inner ear, not the retina.
n.2: Rods work in dim light, give black-and-white vision and serve peripheral vision; they are not concentrated in the fovea.
n.3: Bipolar neurons in the retina pass signals along, but they are not the photoreceptors that detect light.

S.q: While jogging on a hot afternoon, a person's body temperature starts to rise. Which pair of skin responses is mainly responsible for releasing the excess heat?
o: Dermal vessels constrict; eccrine glands secrete sweat
Dermal vessels constrict; arrector pili muscles contract
Dermal vessels dilate; eccrine glands secrete sweat
Dermal vessels dilate; apocrine glands secrete sweat
S.w: To lose heat, dermal blood vessels dilate so more warm blood reaches the surface, and eccrine glands secrete watery sweat that cools the skin as it evaporates.

n.0: Constriction of dermal vessels conserves heat, the opposite of what is needed here.
n.1: Vessel constriction and arrector pili contraction are heat-conserving responses to cold.
n.3: Apocrine glands in the axillae and groin respond mainly to stress and puberty; eccrine glands are the main thermoregulators.

S.q: The first heart sound, S1 ("lub"), is produced by which event in the cardiac cycle?
o: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the start of diastole
Closure of the tricuspid and mitral valves as ventricular systole begins
Opening of the aortic and pulmonary valves as the ventricles eject
Contraction of the atria at the end of ventricular filling
S.w: S1 ("lub") is the sound of the atrioventricular valves (tricuspid and mitral) closing as the ventricles begin to contract. S2 ("dub") is the semilunar valves closing.

n.0: Closure of the semilunar valves at the start of diastole produces S2 ("dub"), not S1.
n.2: Normal heart sounds come from valves closing, not opening.
n.3: Atrial contraction tops up ventricular filling but is not the source of S1.

E.q: The provider explained to an older patient that her bone pain was caused by osteomalacia linked to low vitamin D levels. Based on its word parts, what does osteomalacia mean?
o: Inflammation of the bones
Softening of the bones
Hardening of the bones
Softening of the cartilage
E.w: oste/o means bone and -malacia means softening, so osteomalacia is softening of the bones.

n.0: Inflammation is -itis (osteitis).
n.2: Hardening is -sclerosis, not -malacia.
n.3: Cartilage is chondr/o (chondromalacia); oste/o means bone.

E.q: A home care agency is revising a client letter. Which sentence is written in standard English with no double negative?
o: The aide hadn't scarcely finished charting when the call light came on.
The patient can't hardly sit up in bed without help from staff.
The pharmacy didn't have any of the brand-name tablets in stock.
There isn't no reason for the patient to skip the follow-up visit.
E.w: One negative is enough. "Didn't" is negative and "any" is neutral, so the sentence is correct.

n.0: "Scarcely" is negative in meaning, so "hadn't scarcely" is a double negative; use "had scarcely."
n.1: "Hardly" is already negative, so "can't hardly" is a double negative; use "can hardly."
n.3: "Isn't" and "no" are two negatives; use "There is no reason" or "There isn't any reason."

E.q: A patient is writing to a hospital billing office to dispute a charge. Which sentence best meets the purpose and the audience?
o: Please remove the $85 charge for the March 4 visit, which my insurer paid.
I am writing to you about some issues I have had lately with things on my bill.
Your careless office billed me $85 for March 4, though my insurer paid it.
Hey, quick thing: that $85 charge from March 4 should go, since insurance paid.
E.w: A dispute letter should be courteous and specific: name the charge, the date and the requested action.

n.1: The sentence is polite but vague; it never says which charge is wrong or what should happen.
n.2: The facts are specific, but calling the office "careless" is accusing and likely to make the reader defensive.
n.3: The facts are specific, but "Hey, quick thing" is too casual for a letter to a billing office.

E.q: Read the sentence: "The patient seemed anxious before surgery." What part of speech is "anxious" in this sentence?
o: Adjective modifying "patient"
Noun acting as a subject complement
Adverb modifying "seemed"
Verb completing "seemed"
E.w: "Seemed" is a linking verb, so the word after it describes the subject: "anxious" is a predicate adjective describing "patient".

n.1: "Anxious" describes the patient rather than naming something; a noun complement would rename the subject (for example, "seemed a calm patient").
n.2: After a linking verb the describing word modifies the subject (a noun), so it is an adjective; the adverb form would be "anxiously".
n.3: The whole verb is "seemed"; "anxious" is not a verb form, so it cannot complete the verb.

E.q: A clinic's front-desk sign is being revised. Which sentence uses possessive pronouns correctly?
o: The clinic updated it's hours, and the new schedule is yours.
The clinic updated its' hours, and the new schedule is yours.
The clinic updated its hours, and the new schedule is your's.
The clinic updated its hours, and the new schedule is yours.
E.w: Possessive pronouns (its, yours, hers, ours, theirs, whose) never take an apostrophe.

n.0: "It's" means "it is" or "it has"; the possessive is "its".
n.1: "Its'" is not a word; the possessive pronoun is "its".
n.2: "Yours" is a possessive pronoun and takes no apostrophe.

E.q: A city health department is writing a press release about a safety event. Which sentence uses inclusive, gender-neutral job titles?
o: The firefighters and policemen met with the council chair.
The firefighters and police officers met with the council chair.
The firefighters and police officers met with the council chairman.
The firemen and police officers met with the council chair.
E.w: Bias-free writing uses titles that fit any gender: firefighter, police officer, chair or chairperson.

n.0: "Policemen" is a gendered title; the neutral term is "police officers."
n.2: "Chairman" is a gendered title; the neutral term is "chair" or "chairperson."
n.3: "Firemen" is a gendered title; the neutral term is "firefighters."

E.q: A nursing instructor praised a student for showing empathy while talking with a grieving family. Based on its root, empathy is most closely related to which idea?
o: Feeling
Mind
Love
Knowledge
E.w: The root path means feeling (and also disease), so empathy is the ability to share or understand another person's feelings.

n.1: Mind is the meaning of psych (as in psychology).
n.2: Love is the meaning of phil (as in philanthropy).
n.3: Knowledge is the meaning of cogn (as in cognitive).

E.q: A research summary reads: "The trial drug lowered blood pressure in most participants. ___, several participants reported dizziness and headaches." Which transitions could correctly fill the blank? Select all that apply.
o: For instance
Therefore
Similarly
However
On the other hand
E.w: The second sentence presents a drawback that contrasts with the benefit in the first. "However" and "On the other hand" both signal contrast.

n.0: "For instance" introduces an example of the first sentence, but side effects are not an example of lower blood pressure.
n.1: "Therefore" signals a result, but the side effects are not a consequence of the blood pressure falling in this passage.
n.2: "Similarly" signals a matching point, but a drawback does not match a benefit.

E.q: Original: "Patients who walk within 24 hours after surgery tend to recover faster." A student writes, "Getting patients walking within a day of surgery tends to speed their recovery," with no citation. Which statement is correct?
o: It is plagiarism, since the borrowed idea is not credited
It is patchwriting, since it keeps the original's exact wording
It is acceptable, since the claim counts as common knowledge
It is acceptable, since paraphrased ideas need no citation
E.w: Step 1: the student changed the wording and structure, so this is a paraphrase, not copied text. Step 2: a paraphrase still uses someone else's idea, so it must be cited; without a citation it is plagiarism.

n.1: The wording and sentence structure have been changed, so this is not patchwriting; the problem is the missing citation.
n.2: A specific research finding about recovery after surgery is not common knowledge, so it needs a citation.
n.3: Paraphrases must be cited, because the idea still comes from the source.

E.q: A writing center handout gives six sentences. Which sentences use semicolons and colons correctly? Select all that apply.
o: The tour visits Dayton, Ohio; Erie, Pennsylvania; and Gary, Indiana.
The forms are: the consent, the history, and the release.
The vote was postponed; because the meeting ran late.
Although the meeting ran late; the vote was held.
The kit has one gap: no sterile gloves.
The meeting ran late; therefore, the vote was postponed.
E.w: A semicolon with a conjunctive adverb joins independent clauses; a colon after a complete clause introduces an explanation; semicolons separate series items that contain commas.

n.1: A colon must not come directly after a verb such as "are".
n.2: "Because the meeting ran late" is a dependent clause; a semicolon must join two independent clauses.
n.3: "Although the meeting ran late" is a dependent clause, so a comma, not a semicolon, should follow it.

E.q: A student's paragraph argues that hospitals should serve healthier food in their cafeterias. Which sentence would best conclude the paragraph?
o: Some hospitals currently serve meals from national fast-food chains in their lobbies.
First, cafeterias should add more fresh vegetables and whole grains to each meal.
Hospital parking fees are another issue that deserves attention from administrators.
Healthier menus would let hospitals model the habits they urge patients to adopt.
E.w: A strong concluding sentence restates or extends the paragraph's main point without adding a new topic.

n.0: This sentence is a supporting detail, not a conclusion that wraps up the argument.
n.1: "First" signals the start of a list of supporting points, which belongs in the body of the paragraph.
n.2: This sentence introduces a new topic (parking) instead of closing the argument about food.

E.q: A community health newsletter describes a local clinic. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: Riverside Clinic, which opened in 2020, now offers evening hours.
Riverside Clinic, which opened in 2020 now offers evening hours.
Riverside Clinic which opened in 2020, now offers evening hours.
Riverside Clinic which opened in 2020 now offers evening hours.
E.w: A proper noun is already identified, so the clause "which opened in 2020" is nonessential and needs a pair of commas.

n.1: The closing comma after "2020" is missing.
n.2: The opening comma after "Riverside Clinic" is missing.
n.3: A nonessential clause after a proper noun must be set off with commas.

E.q: From across the room, the respiratory therapist noted that the patient's wheezing was audible without a stethoscope. Based on its root, what does audible mean?
o: Able to be spoken
Able to be seen
Able to be heard
Able to be felt
E.w: The root aud means hear, and -ible means able to be, so audible means able to be heard.

n.0: Speaking comes from voc (voice) or dict (say), not aud.
n.1: Able to be seen is visible, from the root vis/vid (see).
n.3: Able to be felt would come from sens/sent (feel), as in sensory.

E.q: Read the word groups from a medication note: "Because the patient was allergic to penicillin. The doctor prescribed a different antibiotic." Which revision correctly fixes the fragment?
o: Because the patient was allergic to penicillin, the doctor prescribed a different antibiotic.
Because the patient was allergic to penicillin; the doctor prescribed a different antibiotic.
Because the patient was allergic to penicillin the doctor, prescribed a different antibiotic.
The patient was allergic to penicillin, the doctor prescribed a different antibiotic.
E.w: The dependent clause (Because ... penicillin) is attached to the independent clause with a comma, giving a correct complex sentence.

n.1: A semicolon must join two independent clauses; the first part is a dependent clause.
n.2: The comma is misplaced: it separates the subject (the doctor) from its verb, and the comma after the introductory clause is missing.
n.3: Removing "Because" leaves two independent clauses joined by only a comma: a comma splice.

E.q: In anatomy lab, each pair of students began the dissection of a preserved frog, following the steps in the lab manual. Based on all of its word parts, what does dissection mean?
o: To cut apart a specimen for study
The act of cutting apart for study
The study of how living things work
A tool used to cut apart a specimen
E.w: Step 1: dis- means apart and sect means cut. Step 2: -tion forms a noun naming an act or process. Dissection is the act of cutting something apart (for study).

n.0: This defines the verb dissect; the -tion suffix makes dissection a noun.
n.2: The study of living things is biology (bio + -logy), and the word has no part meaning study.
n.3: -tion names an act or process, not a tool (the tool is a scalpel).

E.q: A staff newsletter reports on a wellness program. Which sentence uses hyphens correctly?
o: Twenty-one nurses joined the self care workshop this year.
Twenty one nurses joined the self-care workshop this year.
Twenty-one nurses joined the selfcare workshop this year.
Twenty-one nurses joined the self-care workshop this year.
E.w: Compound numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine are hyphenated, and the prefix self- always takes a hyphen (self-care).

n.0: The prefix self- is joined with a hyphen, and the compound modifies the noun "workshop".
n.1: Compound numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine take a hyphen.
n.2: The prefix self- is joined with a hyphen, not closed up.

E.q: A writing tutor gives a student six sentences from patient handouts. Which sentences are punctuated correctly? Select all that apply.
o: The new nurse on the night shift, works weekends.
I stayed late, but, the charts were still unfinished.
The new nurse on the night shift works weekends.
She needs rest, not more medication.
The forms, that you signed, are in the file.
Mr. Ruiz, your lab results are ready.
E.w: A long subject takes no comma before its verb; a contrasting element (not more medication) is set off by a comma; a name in direct address (Mr. Ruiz) is set off by a comma.

n.0: A comma must not separate the subject (The new nurse on the night shift) from its verb.
n.1: No comma follows a coordinating conjunction; only the comma before "but" is needed.
n.4: A "that" clause is essential (restrictive), so it takes no commas.

E.q: A charge nurse is proofreading a sentence for a unit memo. Which version of the sentence is spelled correctly?
o: She was carrying the foreign samples to the lab.
She was carriing the foreign samples to the lab.
She was carrying the foriegn samples to the lab.
She was carriing the foriegn samples to the lab.
E.w: Two rules apply. Before -ing, a final y is kept (carry + ing = carrying). "Foreign" is an exception to i before e and is spelled e-i.

n.1: "Carriing" wrongly changes y to i before -ing; the y is kept: "carrying".
n.2: "Foreign" is an exception spelled e-i, not i-e.
n.3: Both words are wrong: the y must stay before -ing, and "foreign" is spelled e-i.

E.q: A student is editing a peer's care-plan summary. Which sentence uses adjectives and adverbs correctly?
o: After a night of rest, Jordan felt well enough to go to class.
The new graduate handled the emergency calm and careful.
The cafeteria soup tasted differently after the new cook started.
The team did real good on the state safety inspection this year.
E.w: "Well" can be an adjective meaning "in good health," so "felt well" is correct after the linking verb "felt."

n.1: "Calm" and "careful" describe how she handled it, so they modify a verb and must be adverbs: "calmly and carefully."
n.2: "Tasted" is a linking verb here, so it takes an adjective that describes the soup: "tasted different."
n.3: "Did" is an action verb, so it needs the adverb "well"; "real" should also be the adverb "really."

E.q: A patient leaflet about a vaccine reads: "___ the vaccine can cause a sore arm, most patients find this side effect mild and brief." Which word or phrase best completes the sentence?
o: Because
Whenever
Unless
Although
E.w: The sentence concedes a drawback (a sore arm) and then plays it down. "Although" signals concession.

n.0: "Because" signals cause, but a sore arm does not cause the side effect to be mild.
n.1: "Whenever" signals time, which does not fit a possible side effect weighed against its mildness.
n.2: "Unless" signals a condition, which makes the sentence illogical.

E.q: Kayla's first draft of a research paper on nutrition labels is complete. Place the remaining tasks in the order she should complete them, starting with the first.
o: Reorganize paragraphs and strengthen weak support
Do a final read for typos and missing words
Correct subject-verb agreement and punctuation errors
Submit the final copy to the instructor
E.w: After drafting, the writer revises (reorganizes and strengthens content), then edits (grammar and punctuation), then proofreads (a final check for typos and missing words), and finally publishes (submits the paper). Big-picture changes come first so that later polishing is not wasted on text that gets cut.

E.q: A student is checking notes from a clinical rotation. Which of the following is a fragment?
o: Hoping to finish her charting before the end of the shift.
She hoped to finish her charting before the end of the shift.
Finish your charting before the end of the shift.
Hoping to finish, she charted before the end of the shift.
E.w: Two steps: "Hoping" is a participle, not a main verb, and the word group has no subject, so it cannot stand alone.

n.1: This has a subject (She) and a main verb (hoped), so it is complete.
n.2: This is an imperative sentence; its subject "you" is understood, so it is complete.
n.3: The participial phrase is attached to the independent clause "she charted ...", so it is complete.

E.q: Dr. Shah works in the pediatric unit, where her patients range from newborns to teenagers. Based on the context, what does the word part ped mean in pediatric?
o: Foot
Child
Birth
Bone
E.w: ped can mean foot (pedal) or child (pediatric). The context (patients from newborns to teenagers) shows that here it means child.

n.0: ped can mean foot, as in pedal, but a unit serving newborns to teenagers is about children.
n.2: Birth is natal (as in prenatal), not ped.
n.3: Bone is oste/o, not ped.

E.q: A clinic is updating a flyer for the general public: "Individuals experiencing dyspnea or diaphoresis should seek emergent evaluation." Which revision best suits this audience while keeping the meaning?
o: Persons with respiratory distress or diaphoresis require emergent care.
If you have trouble breathing or heavy sweating, get emergency care now.
If you feel a little bit off, you might think about seeing a doctor.
If you have dyspnea or heavy sweating, get emergency care now.
E.w: Two checks: the revision must use plain words a lay reader knows (trouble breathing, heavy sweating) and keep the message's urgency.

n.0: "Respiratory distress," "diaphoresis" and "emergent" are still medical jargon for lay readers.
n.2: This version loses the specific symptoms and the urgency, so it changes the meaning.
n.3: The urgency is kept, but "dyspnea" is still a medical term that lay readers may not know.

E.q: Because the medication is contraindicated during pregnancy, the pharmacist called the provider to suggest a different drug for the patient. Based on its prefix and the context, what does contraindicated mean?
o: Advised before other treatment
Advised again after a review
Advised together with another drug
Advised against for a patient
E.w: contra- means against, and the context (the pharmacist seeks a different drug) confirms it: a contraindicated drug is one advised against for that patient or situation.

n.0: Before is ante- or pre-, not contra-.
n.1: Again is re-, not contra-.
n.2: Together with is co-, com- or con-, not contra-; the pharmacist is replacing the drug, not adding one.

E.q: A hospital kitchen supervisor is writing a short inventory note. Which sentence uses the correct plural form of every noun?
o: The chefs stored the knives on the shelfs.
The chefs stored the knifes on the shelves.
The cheves stored the knives on the shelves.
The chefs stored the knives on the shelves.
E.w: Many nouns ending in f or fe change to -ves (knife to knives, shelf to shelves), but some simply add s, including chef (chefs).

n.0: Shelf changes f to ves: "shelves".
n.1: Knife changes fe to ves: "knives".
n.2: Chef is an exception to the f-to-ves rule; its plural is "chefs".

E.q: A tutor gives a student six sentences to check for commonly confused words. In which sentences is every word used correctly? Select all that apply.
o: The storm is imminent, so stay indoors.
Her new shoes are to tight to wear.
The elicit drugs were seized at the border.
He gave me some good advise yesterday.
She is conscious of the risks involved.
Please cite your sources in the report.
E.w: "Imminent" means about to happen, "conscious" means aware, and "cite" means to quote or name a source.

n.1: "Excessively tight" requires "too": "too tight to wear".
n.2: Illegal drugs are "illicit"; "elicit" means to draw out.
n.3: After "some good" a noun is needed: "advice". "Advise" is a verb.

E.q: A pharmacy newsletter describes the work of a pharmacist and her intern. Which of the following is a simple sentence?
o: The pharmacist counted the pills while her intern labeled them.
The pharmacist and her intern counted, sorted, and labeled the pills.
The pharmacist counted the pills, and her intern labeled them.
After the pharmacist counted the pills, the intern labeled them, and they left.
E.w: A simple sentence has exactly one independent clause. A compound subject (pharmacist and intern) and a series of verbs (counted, sorted, and labeled) still form one clause.

n.0: "While her intern labeled them" is a dependent clause, so the sentence is complex.
n.2: Two independent clauses joined by ", and" make a compound sentence.
n.3: Two independent clauses plus the dependent clause "After the pharmacist counted the pills" make it compound-complex.

E.q: A clinic receptionist is writing questions for a new front-desk guide. Which sentence uses who or whom correctly?
o: The student whom earned the top score will speak at graduation.
Whom do you think will be named the new charge nurse?
To whom should I send the completed insurance forms?
Whom is responsible for the night count of controlled drugs?
E.w: "Whom" is the objective form. In "To whom should I send," the pronoun is the object of the preposition "to" (send them to him), so "whom" is correct.

n.0: The pronoun is the subject of "earned" (she earned), so it must be "who."
n.1: Ignore "do you think": the pronoun is the subject of "will be named" (he will be named), so it must be "Who."
n.3: The pronoun is the subject of "is responsible" (he is responsible), so it must be "Who."

E.q: Imani is planning the overall structure of an essay on community health fairs. Place the parts of the essay in the order they usually appear, starting with the first.
o: A conclusion that restates the thesis in new words
Body paragraphs that each develop one main point
Background on the topic
A hook that captures the reader's interest
The thesis statement
E.w: The introduction opens with a hook, gives background, and ends with the thesis. The body paragraphs follow, each with a topic sentence linked to the thesis. The conclusion restates the thesis in new words and sums up, with no new evidence.

E.q: A student is labeling word groups taken from a patient education leaflet. Which group of words is a dependent clause?
o: during the long night shift
the nurse finished her charting
running down the hospital hallway
because the pharmacy was closed
E.w: A dependent clause has a subject and a verb (the pharmacy was) but begins with a subordinating conjunction (because), so it cannot stand alone.

n.0: This is a prepositional phrase: it has no subject-verb pair.
n.1: This has a subject and verb and expresses a complete thought, so it is an independent clause.
n.2: This is a participial phrase: "running" is a verbal with no subject.

E.q: Read the sentence from a quality report: "Since the new reminder policy started, the clinic has saw fewer missed appointments." Which revision corrects the verb error?
o: Change "has saw" to "seen."
Change "has saw" to "have seen."
Change "has saw" to "has seen."
Change "has saw" to "had saw."
E.w: Two steps: "since" calls for the present perfect, and a singular subject ("clinic") takes "has" + the past participle "seen."

n.0: A past participle cannot stand alone as the main verb; it needs "has."
n.1: "Seen" is right, but "clinic" is singular, so the helping verb must stay "has."
n.3: "Saw" is the simple past and cannot follow any helping verb; the participle is "seen."

E.q: A charge nurse must tell a coworker that a medication dose was charted at the wrong time. Which sentence has the most appropriate tone?
o: How could you possibly mess up something as basic as charting a dose?
Not to be picky, but charting is kind of a big deal, you know what I mean?
Someone on this shift, and I won't say who, charted a dose at the wrong time.
I noticed the 9 a.m. dose was charted at 11 a.m.; can we fix it together?
E.w: Professional feedback is specific, respectful and focused on solving the problem.

n.0: The scolding question is condescending and likely to make the coworker defensive.
n.1: The passive-aggressive, casual phrasing is vague and unprofessional.
n.2: Hinting instead of speaking directly is indirect and can feel like public blame.

E.q: A student quotes a nurse who said, "He refused the medication twice." The student wants to show that "He" means Mr. Diaz. Which version of the quotation is punctuated correctly?
o: "He (Mr. Diaz) refused the medication twice."
"He [Mr. Diaz] refused the medication twice."
"He, Mr. Diaz, refused the medication twice."
"He refused the medication twice [sic]."
E.w: Brackets mark words the writer inserts into someone else's quotation to clarify it.

n.0: Parentheses inside a quotation signal the speaker's own words, not the writer's insertion.
n.2: Commas would present "Mr. Diaz" as part of what the nurse said, changing the quotation.
n.3: [sic] marks an error in the original quotation; this quotation has no error and the name is still not added.

E.q: A student is writing a report on handwashing habits in a school cafeteria. Place the steps in the order the student should complete them, starting with the first.
o: Submit the final copy
Revise the draft's content and organization
Edit the draft for grammar and punctuation
Organize the ideas into an outline
Write a first draft from the outline
Brainstorm a list of ideas about the topic
E.w: Brainstorming and then outlining are both prewriting (generate ideas, then organize them). Drafting turns the outline into paragraphs. Revising fixes the big picture, editing then fixes sentence-level errors, and publishing (submitting the final copy) comes last.

E.q: Devon is preparing the final copy of a report on campus flu shots. Which of the following tasks belongs to the editing stage rather than the revising stage?
o: Adding a statistic to support the second main point
Fixing a pronoun that disagrees with its antecedent
Reordering paragraphs so the strongest point is last
Removing a sentence that is off topic for its paragraph
E.w: Editing deals with sentence-level correctness: grammar, usage, punctuation, spelling and consistency. A pronoun-antecedent agreement error is a grammar problem, so fixing it is editing.

n.0: Adding support changes the content of the report, which is revising (add).
n.2: Reordering paragraphs changes the organization, which is revising (rearrange).
n.3: Cutting an off-topic sentence improves unity and content, which is revising (remove).

E.q: A patient satisfaction survey summary is being edited. Which sentence uses an adjective correctly after a linking verb?
o: The coffee in the staff break room tastes bitter today.
The infant is breathing good now that the fever has broken.
Their new manager seems nicely, and the staff likes her a lot.
The cafeteria food tastes differently since the new cook started.
E.w: Linking verbs (taste, seem, feel, look, smell) connect the subject to an adjective that describes it: the coffee tastes bitter.

n.1: "Breathing" is an action, so it needs the adverb "well," not the adjective "good."
n.2: "Seems" is a linking verb, so it takes the adjective "nice," not the adverb "nicely."
n.3: "Tastes" links the food to a description, so it needs the adjective "different," not the adverb.
